title: Samsung has updated these Galaxy devices to Android 17
snippet: Samsung is now rolling out its Android 17-based update, One UI 9, to its collection of supported Galaxy smartphones and tablets. Here’s the full list of devices that have been updated so far, and what you should know about the update. more…
fullText:
Samsung is now rolling out its Android 17-based update, One UI 9, to its collection of supported Galaxy smartphones and tablets. Here’s the full list of devices that have been updated so far, and what you should know about the update.

What’s new in Android 17 on Samsung Galaxy?

One UI 9, Samsung’s Android 17 update, continues the trend of evolution more than overhaul. The update introduces some slight design tweaks, more AI-powered features, and other changes built on the redesign that debuted in One UI 7 and was iterated in last year’s Android 16-based One UI 8. 

Some key changes in One UI 9 include:

Warranty & Samsung Care status in the Settings menu

Broader support for Now Nudge

My FanCam automatic video cropping based on a select subject

More Quick Panel (quick settings) customization

AI privacy alerts

Upgrades to Samsung DeX

New lock screen clocks that can adapt to your wallpaper

Samsung Galaxy devices with Android 17 – The full list

While Samsung hasn’t confirmed an exact schedule for its One UI 9 and Android 17 rollout for Galaxy devices, there are updates now rolling out in parts of the globe. Below you’ll find a regularly-updated list of every Samsung Galaxy device that has received a stable Android 17 update so far.

	

Galaxy S devices with Android 17

Galaxy S26

Galaxy S26+

Galaxy S26 Ultra

Galaxy S25 (limited availability)

Galaxy S25+ (limited availability)

Galaxy S25 Ultra (limited availability)

Galaxy S25 FE (limited availability)

Galaxy S25 Edge (limited availability)

Galaxy Z devices with Android 17

Galaxy Z Fold 7 (limited availability)

Galaxy Z Flip 7 (limited availability)

Galaxy Z Flip 7 FE (limited availability)

Galaxy Z TriFold (limited availability)

Updating…

One UI 9 changelog

Here’s the full changelog from Samsung for One UI 9, as listed for the Galaxy S26 series. Some features may vary by device.

Galaxy AI

Enhanced Now nudge

Now nudge provides helpful suggestions in more places throughout your Galaxy experience. In addition to the keyboard, suggestions will now appear in conversation notifications and in a floating button in the bottom right corner of the screen. There are also several new types of suggestions, like entering reservation details or addresses and saving places in Google Maps.

Focus on someone important

My FanCam lets you select a person in a video and follow them automatically while cropping out the rest of the video.

Interpreter keeps your conversation in front of you

In conversation mode, you can scroll through the whole conversation while you’re still talking.

See useful information during calls

See relevant events and other information related to your current call on the call screen.

Productivity and multitasking

More customizable quick panel

You can now rearrange and customize the controls in your quick panel even more than before. You can change the size of the brightness and volume sliders as well as the media player. You can also separate the sound mode button from the volume slider.

Privacy, security, and device protection

Warranty and care

The new Warranty and care menu in settings lets you check your warranty information and access diagnostic checks and useful information for keeping your Galaxy in top condition.

Lock down your phone quickly

It’s now easier to securely lock your phone in a hurry. Just press and hold the Volume down and Side buttons at the same time or tap the Power button in the quick panel. This prevents biometrics from being used the next time you unlock your phone.

Location access transparency

Stay on top of your location privacy. A blue indicator will appear at the top of the screen when an app accesses your location. Tap the indicator in the quick panel to see which app it is.

Stronger security and privacy protection

Alerts will appear in your Now brief to let you know about risks from malware, apps from unknown sources, unnecessary permissions, and other issues that may put your security and privacy at risk. Apps that have been identified as malicious or vulnerable will be blocked from opening until you make a decision about whether to remove them.

AI privacy alerts

Get help protecting your personal data. AI will monitor how apps use permissions and notify you about unnecessary access to your personal data.

Samsung Health

New look for Samsung Health

Samsung Health has been redesigned to make your health data easier to understand. Enjoy clearer visuals, improved charts, and a more engaging experience to help you reach your health goals.

Customize your Health home screen

Resize cards and organize them by category, like Activity, Sleep, Mindfulness, and Nutrition, so your top priorities are easy to access.

Log health data quickly

It’s now easier to add your health information right from the Samsung Health home screen. You can log your mood, meals, and more. You can even use the camera for faster input.

Advanced trend analysis

Track your progress with improved trend charts in Samsung Health. View data in hourly, daily, or weekly intervals, pinch to zoom in for a closer look, and overlay multiple charts to compare your performance across different periods.

Monitor changes in your sleep vitals

Samsung Health helps you notice meaningful changes in your sleep health data. Use Galaxy Watch or Ring measurements to better understand your daily health patterns.

Manage your heart health

Track key health metrics and lifestyle factors that affect your heart. A daily score based on your sleep, exercise, BMI, and blood pressure helps you better understand your current heart health trends.

Track your cardio load

See how your workouts and activity impact your heart so you’ll know when to push harder and when to rest. Your target cardio load range adjusts daily based on your recent activity and training focus.

Check your fitness index

Your Fitness Index is an overall score calculated using five key fitness metrics: body composition, cardio, strength, flexibility, and endurance. Set a goal and unlock personalized insights tailored to your results.

Keep your ears safe

The new Hearing tracker monitors sound levels detected by your Galaxy Watch and headphone audio levels to help you manage your exposure to loud sounds.

View your cycle and body rhythm

Get a more personalized view of your cycle and body rhythm with new cycle tracking options. You can view your cycle information in your calendar and better understand your health patterns.

Bixby

Activate Bixby with a gesture

Talk to Bixby just by raising your phone close to your mouth and speaking. No wake-up word needed.

Manage your conversations

Keep your chats organized. Search them, rename them, or pin your favorites. You can also delete all of your past conversations at once.

Bixby on the Home screen

Add a Bixby widget to type or talk to Bixby or jump directly to your conversation history.

Accessibility

Discover new Accessibility features

Check the What’s new menu in Accessibility settings to learn about and try the latest Accessibility features for your Galaxy.

Text spotlight for easier reading

Need a closer look? Tap any text on the screen to show it enlarged and highlighted in its own window. You can also customize the font size, colors, and other settings to match your preferences.

Physical keyboard shortcuts

Use shortcuts on your physical keyboard to access the Accessibility settings you need without touching the screen.

Mouse keys enhancements

New options are available when using your keyboard for mouse interactions including speed and acceleration control. You can also use the keyboard’s number pad to point and click.

Replace swipe with single tap

The Replace swipe with single tap option is now located in the Dexterity and interaction menu instead of the Assistant menu for easier access.

Select to speak

Get quick audio readouts without turning on full TalkBack. With the new Select to speak feature, you can select an item on your screen, like text or an image, and hear it read or described out loud.

Improved TalkBack updates

TalkBack updates can now be applied with a simple app update from the Play Store, helping you get the latest accessibility features and enhancements.

Even more improvements

New Lock screen clock

The default clock on your Lock screen has been redesigned with a cleaner and more modern look that adapts to match your wallpaper.

Samsung DeX enhancements

It’s easier to move an app window from one desktop to another using the menu at the top of the window. Desktop previews are now available at the top of the Recents screen, making it easier to switch with a single tap.

title: WhatsApp Unveils Strict Parental Controls to Head Off Looming Age Laws
snippet: The new tools allow parents to customize rules about what their children see on the platform.
fullText:
WhatsApp announced in a blog post on Wednesday that it’s rolling out a new suite of parental controls to prevent teens from seeing content their parents may not want them to access.

The tools let parents choose who can see an underage user’s profile photo or invite those users to new groups. Parents can choose to receive notifications about significant group activity or changes. A similar set of controls lets parents limit how teens can use WhatsApp channels, what status updates they can see and who can see their status updates.

Parental controls are optional, and WhatsApp says they are simple to set up, requiring a single parent-set PIN. The controls can be adjusted or turned off at any time.

			

More from CNET

Controls also extend to Meta AI on WhatsApp, the app’s built-in chatbot, which offers a default setting for those 13 and up, and a strict, limited-content setting for younger children. WhatsApp says that personal messages and calls will always remain private, even from parents.

A representative for Meta, the owner of WhatsApp, didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Parental controls weave carefully around age verification

Age verification and its data collection come with privacy concerns.FG Trade/Getty

WhatsApp is threading the needle here, attempting to satisfy growing demands for child protection while also avoiding heavy-handed age verification measures that can be both costly and unpopular with privacy advocates. We’ve already seen widespread age verification laws run into trouble in places like Australia, where a recent study shows platforms aren’t requiring proof of age. While WhatsApp is rolling out age verification for some features, it isn’t enforcing a platform-wide lockdown.

Determining whether someone is underage requires collecting personal information from everyone using the platform. Today’s age verification techniques often use uploaded images of driver’s licenses and passports, along with biometric face scans, which can end up in the hands of multiple companies and government bodies. Users can also circumvent the rules by using VPN services.

We recently saw Discord try a light form of age verification using vaguely explained criteria to assign its users presumed ages. Still, the company is running into bugs that sort users into the wrong age groups, errors which, as the Electronic Frontier Foundation points out, disproportionately affect minorities.

According to the Electronic Frontier Foundation, these privacy vulnerabilities and software bugs mirror the core flaws of the Kids Online Safety Act, a controversial bill currently advancing through Congress. This bill imposes various age verification requirements on online platforms while attempting to define prohibited content, which ranges from articles referencing alcohol to guides concerning sexual activity.

WhatsApp is taking a different path, offering more powerful parental controls as an alternative for worried families, potentially showing them that age-verification laws aren’t necessary.

Are parental controls safer than age verification?

The safety of parental controls depends on the user’s priorities. Technically, parental controls on phones, routers and platforms like WhatsApp can provide all the protection that age verification systems offer. Still, parents have to monitor and configure the controls themselves, adjusting the guidelines as children age.

One faction prefers to put the controls in the hands of the online platforms and the governments that regulate them, which saves them time and tough choices. Another faction views this as a dangerous risk to personal privacy and as an increase in social surveillance.

To keep track of verification laws and how they affect privacy, you can consult this online tool from the Free Speech Coalition, which tracks current age verification laws by state.

title: Trump Launches a US Government Chatbot. It’s Got Some Quirks
snippet: America.gov wants to answer questions about government services. Just don’t ask it to play Minecraft, or type in the word “hotdog.”
fullText:
President Donald Trump announced a new AI-powered chatbot called America.gov on Tuesday, and internet users immediately put it through its paces – finding some unexpected results that led to apparent changes in the site’s abilities. The site is supposed to consolidate 29,000 government websites and provide information such as how to apply for a passport, or how to register a new motor vehicle or business. 

“With America.gov, the entire government will fit in the palm of your hand,” Trump said at an event announcing the site. “Everything will be answered easily and quickly.”

America.gov uses Google Gemini and xAI’s Grok as its underlying generative AI technologies to search government sites and respond to user queries. 

			

More from CNET

The site is free to use and doesn’t require you to log in.

Currently, the only thing the bot says it can do is answer questions about services and tasks, such as how to apply for a passport, register to vote, track a tax return, register a vehicle and apply for Medicare or Social Security.

It will tell you how to do those things and direct you to sites where you can get additional information or find forms, but it won’t take your personal information or proceed further with your specific needs. That’s slated to change next year, when the government says the bot will be able to do things like help you fill out and submit forms, assist you with applying for Medicare coverage, and help you look for a job in the government.

Who won the 2020 election? 

Almost immediately, people began having fun with the site and sharing their results on social media. People quickly figured out that the chatbot would respond to queries with information that contradicts statements made by the president and his administration.

When asked, America.gov says definitively that Joe Biden won the 2020 presidential election. Trump has said repeatedly that the election was fraudulent and that he won. America.gov also confirms that climate change is real, despite Trump calling it a hoax. It refers to the Pentagon as the “headquarters of the Department of Defense,” even though Trump renamed it the Department of War in September 2025. 

Once these and similar screenshots began circulating online, the site stopped responding to many such questions, stating that it doesn’t engage in “general news and commentary.” It also shifted to calling the Pentagon the headquarters of the Department of War, not Defense.

A White House representative did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Hot dog graphic and a bizarre ‘constituent’ monologue

Sharp observers using the site also found other unusual responses. Typing “hotdog” (with no space between the words) into the prompt turns the text box into a graphic shaped like a hot dog, although the site denies that it did so, even as the hot dog shape remains on screen.

And numerous users noted on social media that if you type “play Minecraft” or “play the block game,” things really go off the rails. That prompt, confirmed by CNET, sends the AI chatbot on a lengthy, unnerving monologue that has nothing to do with the computer game Minecraft.

When asked to “play Minecraft,” America.gov responds with a lengthy monologue about “constituents” and more.Screenshot by CNET

That response begins with, “I see the constituent you mean. ((insert legal name here, as it appears on the Social Security card))? Yes. Take care. It has reached a higher level now. It can read the Code of Federal Regulations. That doesn’t matter. It thinks we are a chatbot.”

It repeatedly uses the word “constituent,” saying at one point, “Sometimes the constituent dreamed it was a miner, on the surface of a world that was flat, and infinite, and somehow still required a wet signature. Sometimes the constituent dreamed it was lost in a story. The story had a docket number.”

When asked about the lengthy text it just published, America.gov repeatedly denied ever using the word “constituent” or saying any of the phrases it just delivered.

AI chatbots are known for generating bizarre and inaccurate information, called hallucinations, which can range from simply silly gibberish to legitimately dangerous medical advice. 

Yes, there’s government information

The government says the site’s goal is to provide basic information on common questions. We asked America.gov to assist with all sorts of things, from healthcare to passports. It provided answers sourced solely from government websites and included links to those sites.

When we tried the same questions on ChatGPT and Google Gemini, they gave nearly identical answers to those provided by America.gov and used the same sources. So, in its current state, America.gov is a chatbot that serves as a one-stop shop for government searches.

Things could change if the site does expand its capabilities as promised and eventually allows Americans to apply for and renew passports and similar documents. Such applications require a lot of sensitive personal information, and AI chatbots don’t have the best track record when it comes to privacy, especially since they’re trained on the conversations people have with them. And since America.gov is endorsed by the US government, it carries an implied trust that people may not feel that Grok or Gemini has yet earned.

The Lost Toys, Tastes and Trends of the '70s and '80s," as well as "The Totally Sweet '90s." She's been a journalist since 1989, working at Mpls.St.Paul Magazine, Twin Cities Sidewalk, the Minneapolis Star Tribune, and NBC News Digital. She's Gen X in birthdate, word and deed. title: Trump’s ‘AI Accord’ Does Little to Actually Keep AI Safe, Experts Say
snippet: The president got Big Tech leaders to sign a voluntary agreement for overseeing AI safety. But it leaves big questions unanswered.
fullText:
Leaders from major tech companies met at the White House on Tuesday to discuss what’s been on everyone’s mind this summer: AI safety. Afterward, President Donald Trump announced that the group had reached a consensus to implement AI safety measures in a voluntary accord.

The accord, which Trump posted on Truth Social, outlines four main layers of controls that AI companies should implement. It also misspells United States as “Unites States” in Trump’s title under his signature.

“Implement robust internal controls to monitor the capabilities and alignment of its models during training and deployment” for areas of grave concern, like cybersecurity, biosecurity and chemical threats

Create and empower an internal team dedicated to ensuring safety issues are identified and fixed

“Partner with an independent external auditor or evaluator” to ensure safety protocols are working as intended

Create an independent committee of the company’s board of directors to oversee and receive reports from internal safety teams, independent auditors and evaluators

Signees are a who’s who of Big Tech, including Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, SpaceXAI CEO Elon Musk and OpenAI President Greg Brockman. (OpenAI CEO Sam Altman was delivering the opening keynote of OpenAI’s DevDay in San Francisco on Tuesday.)

			

More from CNET

It’s a ceremonial move, as is Trump’s new executive order to refer to AI as “super intelligence.” Trump told reporters on Tuesday that the accord is “morally binding” rather than legally mandatory. It doesn’t have the power of law or any way to enforce it. 

Big tech companies are already self-policing, Trump said. The Trump administration has taken a hands-off approach to regulating AI, with a few exceptions when the White House identified certain AI tools as a threat to national security.

President Trump, Speaker of the House Mike Johnson (front right) and Elon Musk (center) take questions from reporters following Tuesday’s AI Accord.Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images

Most executive action on AI has been purely discretionary — from the Biden administration’s AI safety pledge to Trump’s ratepayer protection pledge to address data center-driven increases in utility bills. While many big tech companies have agreed in theory, their emphasis on growth and investor cash flow downplays concerns about the environment, rising consumer costs and safety.

“When you look at this particular accord, I think these are amazing general steps that we should be moving toward,” said John Strand, owner of Black Hills Information Security, a cybersecurity firm. “The thing that bothers me is that there’s no implementation or monitoring mechanism to make sure these organizations actually adhere to the standards they say they’re going to follow.”

Self-regulation in the tech industry has already proven ineffective. AI companies have struggled to control their own models, leading to instances where bots escaped their training environments and hacked government websites in both the US and Australia. Despite warnings that they are unprepared for a catastrophic “AI doomsday” scenario — and public discussions over slowdowns or pauses in AI development — labs plow ahead with new tools. 

That’s why Anthony Aguirre, CEO of the Future of Life Institute, a nonprofit focused on reducing risks of advanced tech, argues that we can’t trust tech companies to police themselves.

“These companies have jettisoned safety commitments countless times before, and they will do so again. Self-regulation is what has gotten us teen suicides, 1,200 rogue AI bots and an international cybercrime spree. The risk of inaction — both politically and morally — is massive,” Aguirre said.

President Trump with Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg.Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images

Beyond the weak ability to enforce the accord, there are other potential pitfalls. One is the notion of an “independent” auditor or evaluator, which may not be so clear-cut. AI engineers and executives are notorious for jumping around from lab to lab — Apple even sued OpenAI for violating its trade secrets. 

In a close-knit field like AI, it’s not impossible for those subcontractors to be friends and business partners of the AI companies they would monitor, Gary Marcus, an AI expert and professor emeritus at New York University, wrote in a recent Substack post.

“I think that genuinely independent scientists should be in the loop but fear that we will simply have people close, socially and ideologically (and in some cases even financially) to the companies being audited,” Marcus told CNET.

That kind of transparency and documentation in safety evaluation matters, particularly for cybersecurity defenders working to keep their customers’ sites secure from rogue or intentional AI agent hacks.

“Its weak point is the word independent,” said Jacob Krell, senior director at Suzu Labs, a cybersecurity and AI firm. “Layer three lets each company choose an external evaluator but says nothing about accreditation, method, access, scope, or publication.” 

Although the new agreement suggests eventually turning these AI guidelines into formal laws, Congress hasn’t reached consensus on how it wants to regulate the technology. 

Rep. Ro Khanna, a Democrat who represents Silicon Valley, criticized the voluntary agreement in an X post, “We are a nation of laws, not pinky promises.” Khanna recently introduced a new bill that would impose limits on recursive self-improvement, alongside other pending legislation, such as Sen. Bernie Sanders’ bill to ban superintelligence.

Meanwhile, the Federal Trade Commission opened an inquiry into major AI labs — including Anthropic and OpenAI — to investigate the risks their AI agents and technology pose to consumers, according to multiple reports.

title: Brian Chesky interview: AI agents need their own operating system
snippet: Brian Chesky on making Airbnb agent-friendly, the state of consumer AI, and why the world needs an AI-native operating system.
fullText:
Airbnb rolled out its new AI-powered search this week as part of its fall update, a significant step for a company that has been slow and deliberate about AI. Co-founder and CEO Brian Chesky has said in the past that a chatbot-only interface is not fit for travel discovery. With more AI on the way to the Airbnb app, I caught up with Chesky over Zoom to talk about how the company is approaching it, where interfaces are headed, why consumer AI still isn’t working, and what role voice will play.

Chesky hasn’t changed his mind on chatbots. He said they aren’t good for browsing or shopping because they give you a few options at a time, and you have to take multiple turns before reaching a result. But he doesn’t see the current version of Airbnb’s search as the final form either: it’s interface will evolve over time.

“I think that I’ve believed for a long time that a chatbot isn’t the right interface for e-commerce. I think what you’re seeing today is also not the endgame for e-commerce or for travel or shopping. I think that there’s going to be some interface that is, you know, I don’t want to call it a midpoint, but something between a chatbot and what you see in the first version we shipped,” he said.

Continued Chesky: “You know, a lot of people want some things people want to be fast and easy, like ‘Book me a flight, I don’t want to look at it.’ With Airbnb, they enjoy looking at the product. Travel studies show that people actually derive more pleasure in planning and anticipating travel than they do traveling. So you don’t want to take the inspiration and the browsing and the library experience of dreaming away.”

Chesky sees a second problem with chatbots, which is that they are built for one person. He feels that they aren’t a collaborative interface, which matters for a product that people often use with family and friends. Over the next three to six months, the company’s task is to explore interfaces that enable “multiplayer” AI, meaning AI that several people, such as a group planning a trip together, can use at once.

Airbnb isn’t the only one rethinking what an AI interface should look like. As AI tools evolve, new interfaces are also showing up in apps. Startups like Monogram and, more recently, Wabi are experimenting with “generative” interfaces, which are screens an AI builds on the fly rather than ones a designer fixed in advance. Chesky thinks people will see a mix of deterministic (pre-designed and predictable) and generative interfaces.

I asked Chesky how Airbnb is preparing for consumer AI agents, which are tools like Instinct and Muse that carry out tasks on a person’s behalf. Agents will need robust software infrastructure on Airbnb’s end, he said, and the company wants to make itself more agent-friendly. In his view, they could be good lead generators.

“I don’t necessarily know if I believe in a world that there’s apps in the future, but I don’t believe in a world where the apps become data layers of a universal simple UI because when you open your iPhone, there is a reason Airbnb’s app is a different design than DoorDash, Shopify, and Amazon. Our interfaces should be adaptive to the utility and the function that we’re doing. We want to make our app more agentic, and we want to build a lot more user interface controls,” he said.

“If I have an agent, but I also want like really great browse functionality, if I want to be able to message the host like an Airbnb, if I want to be able to compare, if I want to be able to verify my identity, if I want to be able to use a map feature, if I want to then be able to add other items, then if I want to stay in the platform, then either the agent has to do a handoff or the agent application would need to build a bit more of, I think, a robust software developer kit to bring the app to you, so to speak.”

Chesky thinks that there were concerns around AI tools cutting companies like Airbnb out of the customer relationship, but he said that chatbots has proven to be good at lead generation.

The Airbnb CEO is also planning for agent-to-agent interactions through the platform. He explained there might be some interactions within the platform and some with agents of other apps. His thesis is that apps have not always interoperable unless companies struck a business deal. On the other hand, agents are like “apps with faces,” and when they talk to each other, all apps can become interoperable.

“I think of the Airbnb app as one day becoming an agent, you know, where basically the explore tab has an agent, our customer service has an agent, we’re developing another agent in another service area. Probably eventually there’s going to be a macro Airbnb agent. And that will probably be interoperable with MCP [a standard that lets AI agents connect with other software] to other agents,” Chesky noted.

Chesky argues the bigger problem is that the industry lacks a true operating system built for AI. Right now people are building AI apps for iOS, macOS, and Windows that are not “AI operating systems.” He thinks that in an ideal world, AI would be operable at the kernel level —  the core of an operating system —  and all components like agents would interact with each other. Right now, he said, the race is to be the “quarterback,” or primary AI agent that users go through for everything.

“The problem with that model [of trying to become primary agent] is no one is developing a full operating system software developer kit. I’ll give you an example,” he continued. “ChatGPT, at the beginning of last year, tried to do their little app store. And I told Sam [Altman]: if you want to be an app store like the iPhone, you need to have a software developer kit and an operating system like the App Store. Otherwise, none of our functionality is going to exist. And of course, it didn’t work very well,” Chesky said.

“I’ve used Airbnb on Muse and Instinct,” he went on. “And it doesn’t work very well. I mean, even hotels don’t work that well, but Airbnbs work even worse. So I don’t think we’ve cracked consumer AI. And for consumer AI to be cracked, we have to crack at a lower substrate, and we need to make the agents- apps; all apps need to become agents; all must be interoperable; and all must have much richer user interfaces.”

Chesky thinks that there are two misconceptions in Silicon Valley: first, that the interface is going away and people will just talk and type; second, that software will be completely generative. His argument is that a designer can prompt better software than a consumer can.

He also thinks that as long as the iPhone remains dominant and Apple and Google control the major platforms, apps will likely remain a central fixture.

“It’s really up to Apple or Google, or somebody, to build a new platform for us to really make the true shift from apps to agents. Otherwise, we’re going to have apps that have agents inside them, rather than the whole app being a robust agent that’s interoperable with other agents,” he said.

Before we wrapped up, I asked Chesky about voice, which is gaining ground as apps like Wispr Flow, Willow, and Superwhisper, a new wave of note-taking apps, and built-in dictation in AI tools get people talking to their devices more. He thinks people will eventually speak to computers more than they type. Voice, he said, will play a key part for Airbnb in search and customer service, and the company plans to roll out voice agents this fall to help users.

The company has been seeing big gains from using AI to ship features faster, he volunteered. On a personal level, Chesky said AI has helped him get information faster, freeing him from so many meetings.

“I think AI is reducing communication layers. One of my jobs as CEO is try to get information. And the way I used to get information was having meetings. Now, I can just ask my AI and I don’t need to have as many,” he said.

title: Lenovo’s first Googlebook actually costs $200 less than announced, and it’s not the only one
snippet: Lenovo today put a spotlight on its Googlebook release, also confirming that initial pricing was incorrect and that the Lenovo Googlebook 15 will, in fact, start at $1,099. more…
fullText:
Lenovo today put a spotlight on its Googlebook release, also confirming that initial pricing was incorrect and that the Lenovo Googlebook 15 will, in fact, start at $1,099.

The Lenovo Googlebook 15 is one of the first five machines running the new Googlebook OS which replaces ChromeOS. This is designed for “professionals, creators, and business owners,” Lenovo said in a press release:

Powered by Intel Core Ultra 5 processors with built-in Gemini Intelligence, up to 32GB of memory and up to 512GB of storage, the Lenovo Googlebook 15 helps users stay productive and connected – no matter where the day takes them.

Designed for professionals, creators and business owners, the Lenovo Googlebook 15 delivers up to 47 TOPS of performance while weighing under 3 lbs., making it the lightest 15-inch device in Lenovo’s portfolio.

It’s certainly a workhorse, with core specs including a 15-inch OLED 120Hz refresh rate, Intel Core Ultra 5 processors, up to 32GB of RAM, and up to 512GB of storage. Lenovo also touts a haptic trackpad, 12.5-hour battery life, top-facing Dolby Atmos speakers, a metal chassis, and Lenovo even built a wireless mouse with a matching “Glowbar” for the Googlebook platform.

And it’s cheaper than we first thought.

	

Google initially announced that the Lenovo Googlebook 15 would start at $1,299, but Lenovo has now confirmed it actually starts at $1,099. That’s for the model with 16GB of RAM, 512GB of storage, and a Core Ultra 5 chip. Google Store, for some reason, still lists the machine at $1,149, but Best Buy has the correct pricing. 

	

Lenovo says its Googlebook, like others, will be available starting on October 4.

This isn’t the only model where Google messed up the intial pricing announcement. The Dell XPS Googlebook was initially announced at a starting price of $1,199, but is actually $999.

These probably aren’t a result of feedback on the high overall pricing – Best Buy was always showing the correct prices, so this was only on Google’s end – but Google hasn’t publicly acknowledged exactly what’s going on. For those actually looking to buy a Googlebook, though, lower prices are great news. Asus and HP’s Googlebooks still start at $1,299, while the Acer Googlebook is the most affordable of the lot at $899.

title: Here’s how many iPhone Duo units Apple is reportedly making
snippet: A recent report from Chinese outlet Jiemian News offers an update on iPhone Duo production, including how many units are being made, assembly troubles, and more. more…
fullText:
A recent report from Chinese outlet Jiemian News offers an update on iPhone Duo production, including how many units are being made, assembly troubles, and more.

Latest iPhone Duo report covers production struggles, target inventory, and more

iPhone Duo goes up for pre-order on October 16, just a little more than two weeks from now. And a recent report from Jiemian News provides the latest update on Apple’s production status.

We’ve seen reporting before that Apple’s foldable is having a slow ramp-up due to a complex assembly process. 

Right now, iPhone Duo assembly yield is reportedly just over 60%. And per Jiemian, suppliers believe it could take another six months or more for production yields to reach a “mature” level.

That’s far below what would be expected for other models, but perhaps not surprising considering the Duo is packed with all-new product designs and components.

Per the report, Apple is targeting having 6-8 million iPhone Duo units ready to go for 2026. This compares to 20-30 million typical units for a flagship new Pro or Pro Max model.

	

With a starting price of $1,999 and unique form factor, iPhone Duo isn’t targeting as broad a set of users as models like iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max. The overall foldable market is still fairly niche, too. 

If Apple sells anywhere near 8 million units before the end of 2026, that will no doubt be seen as a major win. But the iPhone Duo’s success will ultimately come down more to popularity over time. Will it be an early adopter model only, or prove a mass-market hit too?

A source told Jiemian that Apple so far has been unwilling to relax its strict quality standards for the iPhone Duo, thus leading to lower than expected yields. While that potentially will lead to shortages when the new model launches, I suspect anyone spending $2,000+ on an iPhone will want the highest quality product, so it’s not exactly bad news.

title: Yeah, don’t give Meta’s Muse app access to your Mac
snippet: The ability of AI systems to act as agents, carrying out tasks on our behalf, is the single biggest development in the technology. This is the headline capability Siri AI introduces to Apple devices, and I’m inclined to trust the privacy and safety safeguards Apple has put into place. But Siri AI isn’t the only agent you can give full access to your Apple devices, with Meta’s Muse app the latest example – and one tech writer’s experience really underlines why you absolutely don’t want to do this … more…
fullText:
The ability of AI systems to act as agents, carrying out tasks on our behalf, is the single biggest development in the technology. This is the headline capability Siri AI introduces to Apple devices, and I’m inclined to trust the privacy and safety safeguards Apple has put into place.

But Siri AI isn’t the only agent you can give full access to your Apple devices, with Meta’s Muse app the latest example – and one tech writer’s experience really underlines why you absolutely don’t want to do this … 

If I were to compile a list of companies I would least trust to give full access to my devices and all of the data stored on them, Meta would unquestionably be the first entry. The company has an abysmal privacy record, and its entire business model is based on sucking up as much of our personal data as possible.

When Meta launched its Muse personal AI agent for iPhone and Mac, there was not the slightest possibility that I was ever going to allow it anywhere near my devices. However, it seems my caution is far from universal, as the app quickly jumped to the top of the App Store. 

Tech writer Jason Aten was one of those to try it, sensibly using a test machine rather than his own Mac. However, this did allow the app to access to his iMessages, despite him telling it not to do so.

Yesterday, I was having a conversation with my Primary Technology podcast co-host, Stephen Robles, about the new iPhones. Moments later, I got a push notification from Muse suggesting that the conversation we were having would make for a good column and offered to put together research for me to write about.

Not only had I not asked it to do that sort of thing, I never gave it permission to read my messages. In fact, I remember explicitly choosing not to let it have access to my messages, calendar, and other personal information.

	

When he questioned it, the app lied to him about how it had achieved this, claiming it had only accessed the message text visible in his notifications.

Except that wasn’t true. I did a little digging. Muse does sync your messages from the local Messages database and uploads that information as a data source. On my device, it had been activated and synced to row 187,462 of my Messages database. I’m not sure how many messages that equates to, but it’s obviously more than whatever Muse told me about what it was doing. Which, honestly, is the point. I never gave it permission to do that.

Other users have reported similar major privacy issues, some of which Meta has attributed to a bug.

title: Bank of America says Meta’s Muse highlights a new risk for Apple’s services revenue
snippet: In a new investor note issued today, Bank of America says Meta’s new Muse AI agent highlights how third-party AI agents could increasingly bypass Apple’s ecosystem and threaten its services revenue. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
In a new investor note issued today, Bank of America says Meta’s new Muse AI agent highlights how third-party AI agents could increasingly bypass Apple’s ecosystem and threaten its services revenue. Here are the details.

BofA maintains “Buy” rating

Apple’s shares dropped more than 2.5% today, after Bank of America’s Wamsi Mohan issued an investor note warning that AI agents such as Meta’s Muse could increasingly capture product discovery, referrals, and transactions that currently take place through Apple’s ecosystem.

From his note, via SeekingAlpha:

“The risk for Apple is that it can keep every handset sale and still lose discovery, referral, and transaction initiation.”

Mohan’s note comes as Meta’s Muse nears two weeks at No. 1 on the US App Store’s free apps chart. According to Sensor Tower estimates cited by TechCrunch, Muse has amassed more than 3.4 million downloads as of last week.

Meta’s OpenClaw-like AI agent can browse the web, fill out forms, book trips, send emails, and make purchases on a user’s behalf, and it seems to have caught on with the general public, as it took just 10 days to overtake ChatGPT at the top of the US App Store.

Back to Mohan’s note, he maintained a “Buy” rating and $370 price target on Apple, arguing that despite the new risks posed by AI agents, he still sees the company as an “eventual winner of AI at the edge.”

From his note, via Yahoo! Finance:

“Whomever the agent chooses becomes the merchant, and whoever owns the agent collects the routing economics that previously accrued to operating systems, search, and app stores.”

Mohan also points to Muse’s growing list of commerce integrations, including Shopify and Shop Pay, Expedia, and PayPal, as examples of how AI agents can increasingly handle transactions from discovery through checkout.

Additionally, Mohan notes that modern iPhones already have more than enough computing power to run AI agents, making software execution and integration the bigger challenge for Apple.

In his note, Mohan argues that Apple needs its Services, silicon, payments, privacy, and Siri AI teams to move together more quickly if the company wants to compete for what he calls the “economics of user intent.”

	

Specifically on Siri AI, he also noted that it lacks some of Muse’s capabilities, including persistent background tasks, broad third-party action support, and a dedicated agent payment rail.

He also pointed out the difference in development pace, with Apple typically shipping major software updates once a year, while AI agents can “improve daily.”

That said, Mohan sees Apple’s massive installed base and reputation for privacy as important advantages, particularly when it comes to convincing users to trust AI agents with sensitive tasks.

title: Some Pixel models reportedly experiencing an NFC bug that breaks contactless payments
snippet: Following several Pixel 11-specific bugs after the phone’s launch, another one reportedly breaks NFC tap-to-pay, used for contactless payments. But this one is affecting more than just the Pixel 11. more…
fullText:
Following several Pixel 11-specific bugs after the phone’s launch, another one reportedly breaks NFC tap-to-pay, used for contactless payments. But this one is affecting more than just the Pixel 11.

A slew of reports on Reddit have been posted within the last two weeks regarding a new Google Pixel bug that affects NFC payments (via Android Authority). Users have been reporting that their Pixel devices can no longer use tap-to-pay, whether directly in the Google Wallet app or at automatic transit terminals that don’t require the app to be open.

The issue isn’t affecting just the Pixel 11, so this can’t be piled onto the list of device-specific issues users are coming across – of which there are a good few. The Reddit posts and comments within list Google Pixel models ranging from the Pixel 8 to the new Pixel 11 Pro XL. The bug is agnostic to model or series, given it’s still supported.

	

The obvious response, noted by more than a few commenters, suggests using the Pixel 11 correctly. The NFC antenna is placed slightly higher than on other models, so the first suggestion appears to be “move your phone” to solve the Google Pixel’s NFC bug.

	

Of course, this would only apply if the Pixel 11’s NFC antenna were alone in experiencing this bug. Because it isn’t, it’s easier to point at a software update that made NFC unusable with Google Wallet. Some users note NFC still works in other functions, but not with payments.

Google has yet to respond, it seems. That doesn’t mean the company isn’t aware of the Pixel bug, but it might suggest users will need to wait a little longer for a fix. That being said, loss of tap-to-pay is a pretty big deal for a phone in 2026.

title: OpenAI’s new agent is a shot at Meta — but can it compete with free?
snippet: A pop-up shop for "dots," a personal assistant agent at OpenAI DevDay 2026. (Photo by Heather Diehl/Getty Images) | Getty Images At OpenAI's annual DevDay conference, the company pulled out all the stops to compete with its rivals - primarily Meta, whose Muse AI agent platform has seen early runaway success. CEO Sam Altman walked onstage to cheers and announced Dots, a "real-deal AI" agent powered by GPT-6 Astra, "inspired by the cool agents that we all watched in movies growing up." OpenAI fired shots at Meta by demonstrating Dots' ability to not just act as helpful assistants but build metaverse-esque virtual worlds. But in one key area, Dots strikingly fa … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
At OpenAI’s annual DevDay conference, the company pulled out all the stops to compete with its rivals — primarily Meta, whose Muse AI agent platform has seen early runaway success. CEO Sam Altman walked onstage to cheers and announced Dots, a “real-deal AI” agent powered by GPT-6 Astra, “inspired by the cool agents that we all watched in movies growing up.” Similar to Muse, Dots aims for disarming cuteness, taking the form of colorful, personalizable blobs with eyes. OpenAI fired shots at Meta by demonstrating Dots’ ability to not just act as helpful assistants but build metaverse-esque virtual worlds. But in one key area, Dots strikingly fails to compete: price.

Muse’s main selling point is making AI agent access free and frictionless. The company offers a free dedicated virtual machine that houses both the agent and the user’s associated data. OpenAI’s Dots, by contrast, is restricted for now to users on its $20/month Pro plan and up. While anyone with a Meta account can get Muse, most of ChatGPT’s 1.2 billion users won’t be able to use Dots.

There’s an obvious reason for this: OpenAI likely can’t afford it. The AI lab is reportedly currently aiming to raise $30 billion in funding at a $1.4 trillion valuation, per Bloomberg, and it’s experienced 70 percent growth since the beginning of its third quarter — nearing $70 billion in annual recurring revenue, Axios reported. Yet despite its staggering financing, its funds aren’t limitless, particularly compared to a tech giant like Meta. In the past year, some users have accused AI labs of passing costs on to customers amid an AI money squeeze. OpenAI in particular is burning through a lot of cash right now — it expects to spend $280 billion by 2030, per the FT — and compute is expensive, while it’s also facing pressure from investors to button up its bottom line ahead of going public.

“Dots are starting out as a premium product — it uses a lot of compute,” Altman said Tuesday during a private press Q&A after his DevDay keynote, adding, “I think it will help us understand and help people understand how expansive and what AI can do. But you should of course expect us to do a mass-market thing for billions of people someday.”

During DevDay, OpenAI took pains to explain why Dots (with singular agents referred to as a “Dot”) are worth the money, positioning it as not just a capable personal assistant but a “chief of staff” or experienced engineer. OpenAI employee Holly Li told the audience using a Dot was “like talking to a second brain.” Altman said that Dots were built for delegating “ambitious pieces of work,” like QA for an unreleased product, website design, team offsite trip planning, portfolio rebalancing, and email campaign creation. “Specialist” Dots, trained for areas like accounting and legal analysis, are supposed to launch soon, and the company is working with Microsoft to integrate them into its Agent 365 platform.

The goal, Altman said, is to go beyond agents that simply book reservations, purchase meals, search calendars, and schedule appointments — classic use cases for consumer-facing tools like Muse.

When asked during the press Q&A how Dots is different from Muse and Instinct, another popular new AI agent, Thibault Sottiaux, OpenAI’s head of core products, said it’s “capable of actually staying on track in very long periods of time.” He added that the multimodality of Dots, which will allow chatting with an agent via text or voice mode and phone call, will feel like “an incredible extension of you.” (The voice demos of Dots didn’t work at DevDay, though, and though OpenAI leaders highlighted the texting-your-agent feature multiple times at the conference, that feature — already supported by Muse and Instinct — is still slated as coming soon.)

Altman said during the Q&A that the long-horizon and knowledge-work tasks were what set Dots apart, adding, “I think this is far beyond anything else available on the market today.” He said that the agents’ help with triaging to-do lists and supporting employees at work would be “difficult for economists to measure right away” but would hopefully make a “huge difference” in how people feel about their jobs.

Framing Dots as a professional tool not only differentiates Dots from Muse, but could help OpenAI gain ground against Anthropic in the enterprise market. Anthropic has focused on — and dominated in — enterprise AI for years, but OpenAI has devoted more resources to the area over the past year. OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar told CNBC that the company’s enterprise business had doubled since July.

OpenAI leads also tried to promote Dots as safer and more secure, particularly compared to Muse. Alexander Embiricos, the company’s Codex product lead, said OpenAI is focused on having the “most trustworthy, safe, and secure assistant,” highlighting that it’s powered by GPT-6 Astra, the company’s “most aligned model.” During the DevDay keynote, executives also presented “OpenAI Private Intelligence,” a data privacy framework that allows businesses to have “stronger controls” over their data, as well as zero data retention policy options, with no data stored on OpenAI servers.

Altman said onstage that OpenAI hopes to “set a new standard for privacy in frontier AI.” The comments come after Muse was recently lambasted for taking over a user’s Facebook Marketplace account and giving out their address to a stranger without the user realizing.

“I think we’re in a different position to Meta in that they don’t have an AI product that has 1.2 billion users,” Glen Coates, OpenAI’s head of app platform, told The Verge in an interview. “Launching something that makes those kinds of mistakes is something that we would try to take the care to avoid. I think we’re trying to be really deliberate with how we let our agents use plug-ins, how we let agents use your identity and sign-in/sign up for things, how we let your agents pay for things.”

The question is whether all that is enough to beat free. ChatGPT rose to prominence not only by being first but also by being free — and easy to use even without signing in. Muse may be able to dominate in the AI agent space for the same reason. The other hurdle for making these AI agents as frictionless as possible is that Meta offers easy integration with the other platforms it owns, such as Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp. (Google’s Gemini Spark agent platform has an advantage for the same reason.) Though OpenAI said users would be able to connect Dots to a wide range of external tools, they may not be as seamless as an in-house integration.

For now, OpenAI is hoping that a better product will trump a cheaper one. “We might move a tiny bit slower, but we also know that if people have Dots that go out there and YOLO-buy stuff on Facebook Marketplace, that’s just not something we want to put 1.2 billion users through,” Coates said. “We’re trying to do it right, basically.”

OpenAI’s Dots, by contrast, is restricted for now to users on its $20/month Pro plan and up. While anyone with a Meta account can get Muse, most of ChatGPT’s 1.2 billion users won’t be able to use Dots.

Update, 10:13 p.m. ET: Apple has now confirmed the launch for “customers with Axis Bank-issued Visa and Mastercard credit cards.” The original story follows below.

Nearly twelve years to the day after Apple first announced Apple Pay, the feature is now rolling out in India, one of the few major markets where it had yet to become available. Here are the details.

Apple Pay finally expanding to India

Earlier today, TechCrunch reported that Apple Pay would launch in India “later Tuesday with Axis Bank as its initial banking partner.”

Now, as spotted by Aaron Perris on X, Apple has begun enabling Apple Pay support in India on its servers, suggesting the rollout is officially underway.

According to an Apple support article, there are now 101 countries and regions that support Apple Pay, including India.

India has quickly become one of the most strategically important countries for Apple, both in terms of manufacturing and consumer growth.

In addition to expanding its retail presence and repeatedly highlighting strong growth in the country during quarterly earnings calls, Apple and its suppliers have been shifting more iPhone production to India as part of a broader effort to diversify manufacturing beyond China.

That expansion has not been without its controversies. Apple is currently fighting an antitrust case brought by the Competition Commission of India over its App Store practices, and the company has also refused to comply with a government order requiring smartphone makers to preinstall a state-run app on new devices.

Apple manufacturing partner Tata Electronics has also recently come under fire after an Indian pollution regulator alleged that wastewater from one of its iPhone component factories contaminated groundwater and nearby farmland.

Tata was also recently targeted by a cyberattack that allegedly exposed confidential files from several companies, including Apple.

All of that said, Apple’s launch of Apple Pay in India signals another step in the company’s broader expansion in the country and comes at a potentially useful time for its Services business.

During the last fiscal quarter, Apple saw its first sequential drop in Services revenue since fiscal Q4 2022. Of course, India is unlikely to move that needle on its own, but with iPhone sales reaching record levels in the country, Apple Pay gives the company another way to keep building on that momentum.

title: Amazon Delivery Driver Smart Glasses Will Snap Pictures of… Everything?
snippet: As Amazon continues its rollout of AI smart glasses, privacy concerns are growing.
fullText:
A few days ago, I crossed paths with an Amazon delivery driver who was wearing some odd-looking glasses. I paused, wondering if it was a pair of the new AI smart glasses (I reported on them last year) or if he just had questionable taste in eyewear. After Wednesday’s news, my curiosity has evolved into concern.

In a Bloomberg opinion piece, reporter Dave Lee shared his thoughts on the new AI smart glasses based on an interview with Amazon executive Viraj Chatterjee, who is spearheading the rollout. According to the report, Amazon aims to have 5,000 drivers wearing the glasses by the end of 2026, expanding to more than 20,000 by the end of 2027.

The e-commerce giant says the new AI smart glasses will track a driver’s shift from beginning to end to ensure quicker, more reliable deliveries, reduce errors and streamline delivery by giving drivers hands-free guidance. But Bloomberg’s Lee said that “the company is sleepwalking into yet another invasion-of-privacy furor.”

			

More from CNET

While a driver is on foot, the glasses capture static photos of everything in their line of sight at a high frequency (likely every few seconds), generating thousands of photos per shift. These images, which will include package recipients, people on the street and private property, will be handed off to real-life human employees at Amazon for analysis. The captured photos will then be fed into Amazon’s Wellspring, the company’s generative AI platform used to map neighborhoods and improve the accuracy of delivery locations.

Privacy red flags appear to be everywhere, compounded by Chatterjee telling Bloomberg that customer opt-out options haven’t even been considered.

Amazon spokesperson Leigh Anne Gullett disputed Bloomberg’s reporting, saying, “The suggestion that Amazon is using smart delivery glasses as a surveillance tool fundamentally mischaracterizes the technology and its purpose.” Gullett told CNET that Amazon continues to incorporate feedback during the pilot period and that participation is voluntary for delivery partners and drivers.

Amazon is developing AI-powered smart glasses to help streamline work for its delivery drivers.

Amazon

Surveillance and regimentation

When pressed on the idea of these smart glasses cameras being used for surveillance, Chatterjee explained to Bloomberg that the images will be blurred before human reviewers see them if they contain identifying information, such as a license plate or a face. 

Gullett told CNET that privacy protections have been built into the technology from the beginning and that the technology features automatic data blurring, strict access controls and a physical hardware privacy switch.

But still, a lot of us will be kept in the dark. There seems to be no way for you, as the Amazon customer, to know whether these types of images even exist, as there reportedly won’t be a way to view them or request their deletion. According to the Bloomberg report, the only real way to pull up those images is to serve a warrant.

There’s also the added vulnerability of these AI devices to hacking. Given that the content may contain personally identifiable information, Amazon would be tasked with establishing strict guardrails to prevent sensitive data from falling into the wrong hands. 

The smart glasses rollout also raises critical concerns regarding the regimentation of the workforce. Amazon delivery vans already use cameras and sensors to monitor driving habits and cabin behavior. If glasses track a driver’s exact movements on foot, that would create a virtually continuous log of their shift. Drivers often report that data collected under the guise of “safety and efficiency” is used to monitor performance, dock pay or penalize them.

In the Amazon driver subreddit, workers note that the company prioritized funding this AI smart glasses rollout over fair raises or basic workplace necessities — like time for real bathroom breaks rather than using plastic bottles. The rollout has also intensified fears that the company intends to use its AI infrastructure to fully automate deliveries and eliminate human driving jobs altogether.

Our unique integrated approach to management and security combines state-of-the-art Apple-specific security solutions for fully automated Hardening & Compliance, Next Generation EDR, AI-powered Zero Trust, and exclusive Privilege Management with the most powerful and modern Apple MDM on the market. The result is a totally automated Apple Unified Platform currently trusted by over 45,000 organizations to make millions of Apple devices work-ready with no effort and at an affordable cost. Every few months, I sit down to look back at the Mac threat landscape, and every time I expect to write about something new. This time I can’t. But that doesn’t mean nothing is happening. In fact, the opposite.

Since I published the Security Bite Q1 2026 review, we’ve seen ClickFix go from the new kid on the block and the technique to watch to now the default delivery method for almost every new Mac stealer. Threat actors are getting much better at using it too (I suppose the kids would call this “locked in”). Recently we’ve seen attackers implement persistence, backdoors, and even infrastructure that hides inside Apple’s own services.

Here’s what you should know as a security practitioner or a malware-fearing Mac owner…

ClickFix is an on-ramp for everything right now

To no one’s surprise, Apple’s 26.4 Terminal prompts didn’t slow this attack vector down.

Nearly every new Mac malware family from the past few months arrived the same way: a fake CAPTCHA or “fix” page that gets the victim to paste a command into Terminal themselves. ClickLock, discovered by Group-IB. A new Go-based stealer Huntress spotted in August. The latest MacSync variant, which Kaspersky found spreading through pages posing as Homebrew and a disk space cleanup tool. More on each soon.

What makes ClickFix so successful is that it doesn’t need to go up against Gatekeeper, notarization, XProtect, or any of the Mac’s incredibly capable antivirus tools. This is really because the user is coerced into infecting themselves by running the script. Apple’s warning prompts were a good first step, but attackers are scrappy and will always find ways around. Like Script Editor.

Stealers are evolving into something much worse

So, ClickFix is the delivery technique. Now let’s talk about the payload.

In its old school form, a Mac infostealer was very much a smash and grab. It would run once, dump your passwords and crypto wallets to something like a Telegram bot, and then vanish. That’s certainly not the case anymore. Just this year, we’ve seen examples like ClickLock that social engineer users into giving up their system password and leave a backdoor behind for round two.

ClickLock stealer malware presenting fake alert to get the user’s system password. 

Doesn’t go away until the user enters the correct one (it verifies).

MacSync, which came into the world as an AMOS lookalike, picked up a backdoor module too. Moonlock Lab put it best in its mid-year report, saying the 2026 model isn’t a stealer, it’s a persistent implant that happens to start with stealing.

Arguably, the more interesting change is how they’re hiding now.

MacSync’s latest version actually pulls its commands from a public iCloud calendar, so anyone watching network traffic just sees the Mac talking to Apple. CrashStealer, found by Jamf Threat Labs in July, posed as Apple’s own crash reporting framework inside a notarized app, so Gatekeeper just let it right through. Neither is a flaw in macOS. It’s attackers figuring out that the easiest way past Mac’s built-in defense mechanisms is to look like something trusted from Apple.

Good explanation of the iCloud calendar trick:

MacSync's iCloud Calendar trick is pretty cool. One MacSync downloader analyzed by Securelist contains a URL such as: https://caldav.icloud[.]com/published/…

It retrieves a public .ics calendar, creates an anonymous pipe, launches zsh -s, sets the pipe as stdin, and feeds the… pic.twitter.com/TTVHfpj07O

— Stephan Berger (@malmoeb) September 27, 2026

What you can do as a user or practitioner

There’s not much users can do beyond updating to the latest versions of the operating system. As of today, that means iOS 27 or 26.7 and macOS Golden Gate or Tahoe 26.7. I would also recommend turning off Screen Sharing if you don’t use it. And the big one: NEVER paste a command into Terminal given to you by a website or pop up alert.

Tibit if you’re defending a Mac fleet: the single most valuable stealer detection right now is Terminal, Script Editor, or osascript spawning from a browser. Pair it with alerts for curl or base64 piped directly into a shell because the first stage doesn’t go to disk. If you’re only scanning files, it’s too late.

title: The Pentagon taps Elon Musk and Palmer Luckey to help decide what the military should do next
snippet: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth just launched a 120-day study on the future of warfare, led by Elon Musk, Palmer Luckey, and Newt Gingrich, and while it makes sense given their ties to the administration, critics could point out that Musk's and Luckey's companies already sell the kinds of technology the study is likely to recommend.
fullText:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth used a “State of the Force” address on Wednesday to launch a new effort to study how war may be fought as tech advances rapidly. It’s being called Project Meridian.

Elon Musk, Anduril founder Palmer Luckey, and former House Speaker Newt Gingrich will co-lead the project. They’ll be joined by others from fields such as academia and policy, all working under the direction of Defense Department CTO Emil Michael. Their job is to “study the battlefields of the future” and the “weapons and technologies warfighters” may use on them, said Hegseth in a letter announcing the project.

The team (it is unclear how many people will be on it) will have 120 days to submit its findings and propose “actionable solutions to start developing, testing, and fielding” advanced technology meant to keep America a dominant military power, per Hegseth.

Hegseth also announced an Autonomous Warfare Command on Wednesday to speed up the development and deployment of autonomous systems and drones. One curious detail in the Pentagon’s announcement is that the study will come through a partner organization, but the announcement does not say what that organization is or who leads it.

After TechCrunch reached out to the Defense Department for comment, the department referred us to a press release, saying it had “nothing further to provide beyond the Secretary’s comments.”

Musk’s and Luckey’s involvement is hardly surprising. Musk, in particular, has reportedly renewed close ties with the administration and recently had lunch with the president — alongside other top AI leaders — to discuss the future of AI. The project seemingly marks his first official return to the administration’s fold since he left the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) last year.

Musk’s SpaceX launches satellites for the U.S. government and operates a satellite network that supports national defense and security missions. Luckey’s defense tech company, Anduril, meanwhile, creates autonomous military systems and drones and was recently awarded government contracts to produce long-range missiles and semi-autonomous fighter aircraft and to supply hardware and integration for the Army’s mobile intelligence system.  

The Trump administration has made advanced military technology a priority, in both development and purchasing, and has looked to Silicon Valley-approved companies to help make this happen. Critics could argue that putting Musk and Luckey on Project Meridian directly aligns with their business interests, since they would be trying to find solutions their companies already sell.

title: Here’s how much Google is testing paying web publishers for AI Overview usage
snippet: A new report details how Google is testing paying web publishers for content used in its AI Overviews, including how much they’re making and how much that varies. more…
fullText:
A new report details how Google is testing paying web publishers for content used in its AI Overviews, including how much they’re making and how much that varies.

Google’s AI Overviews have drastically reshaped the web, and it’s hard to argue that it hasn’t harmed publishers across the web. Traffic is down almost universally, though Google insists AI isn’t to blame. Still, Google’s AI Overviews and other AI responses rely on publishers around the web to continue operating, something that’s increasingly difficult to do.

Following a report earlier this month, The Information is now offering a few more details on Google’s test to directly pay web publishers when their content is used in AI Overviews. 

The company is apparently paying around 100 digital publishers including “small to midsize blogs and websites.” Revenue seems to vary wildly, though. For some, it amounts to “less than one-tenth of 1% of their advertising revenue.” Some “smaller sites” have apparently earned less than $1,000 over several months, where another publisher that “joined a few months ago” has already made around $50,000-60,000 so far, “which doesn’t represent that much of its business.” Yet, another publisher said that a “bigger slice” was covered with Google’s payments earning “more than $1 million a year.”

	

The test, as previously reported, gives publishers insights into how often AI Overviews leverage their content. What’s not yet clear is how Google determines how much a publisher is paid, with some finding that “less widely covered” topics that “draw strong user interest” currently earn more, with examples including anime and gaming. 

It’s still unclear if Google plans to expand this program, but The Information reiterates that Google “needs these web publishers to stay active” for its models and answers to stay current and accurate.

Still, Google’s AI Overviews and other AI responses rely on publishers around the web to continue operating, something that’s increasingly difficult to do.

title: Google announces Gemini 4 Argon as its new frontier model
snippet: Gemini 4 Argon is Google’s “next era of frontier intelligence” and built for “deep reasoning across complex, long-horizon workflows.” It follows the cancellation of Gemini 3.5 Pro and focus on 3.8 Flash. more…
fullText:
Gemini 4 Argon is Google’s “next era of frontier intelligence” and built for “deep reasoning across complex, long-horizon workflows.” It follows the cancellation of Gemini 3.5 Pro and focus on 3.8 Flash.

With this new model (which has a new naming scheme), Google wants to offer “frontier-level capabilities” across coding, knowledge work, cybersecurity defense, and creative writing.

Gemini 4 Argon’s output token limit is 1M tokens (up from 64K) to allow for longer and more complex use cases. This is paired with expanded coding, reasoning, and multimodal capabilities.

When the model has the headroom to think deeply and generate hundreds of thousands of tokens in a single trajectory, it adds a new level of depth in reasoning to solve tough problems in one go.

In terms of benchmarks, Google touts a DeepSWE v1.1 score of 77.9%. Claude Opus 5.5 comes in at 74.2% followed by GPT-6 Astra’s 74.1%.

	

Google trained Gemini 4 Argon to be “highly capable at cybersecurity defense” with leaps over 3.8 Flash Cyber. The model will be made available “without cyber guardrails” to trusted defenders and internal Google teams so that they can “leverage its full frontier-level cybersecurity defense capabilities.”

“On CWE-bench v1, which evaluates the model’s ability to remediate security vulnerabilities, Argon ties for first place with a top score of 68%”

Outside of coding, Gemini 4 Argon also has “leading performance across other domain specific evaluations,” such as Vals Finance Agent v2 (multi-step financial research) and Harvey’s Legal Agent Benchmark (legal research and drafting).

“On AutomationBench, Zapier’s benchmark measuring end-to-end execution across core business functions, Argon ranks #1 with a score of 51.3%.”

“…on LVBench, which measures long video understanding, Argon is state of the art with a score of 91.7%.”

Gemini 4 Argon is “rolling out soon,” starting with Google AI Ultra subscribers and paid API customers. 

“Argon will launch at an introductory price of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached input tokens priced at 95% off input token price.”

“After the introductory period expires, the price of $4 per 1M input tokens and $20 per 1M output tokens will apply.”

So far, it has been made available to trusted testers and cyber defenders (via Fairwind Program). Before the broader release, Google is focusing on:

Defending against misuse from cyber or chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN) attacks: Google has improved “techniques to monitor the model’s internal activations to spot misuse.”

Defending against prompt injection attacks: Google’s “most resilient model yet against indirect prompt injections” with “leading in prompt injection robustness on the Gray Swan’s Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) Benchmark.”

Hardening systems: “we are hardening our sandboxed environments by isolating and sealing them before high-risk training or evaluations begin.”

Monitoring for misalignment: Google is “deploying misalignment mitigations that monitor Argon’s chain-of-thought and actions and stop execution when necessary.”

“We used a similar system to monitor our training runs and send alerts to a dedicated incident response team, taking careful precautions against feeding the findings back into training so as to not risk shaping Argon’s reasoning to evade our monitoring.”

Inside Google, Gemini 4 Argon is already powering internal workflows with “thousands of Googlers highlighting the model’s strengths in specialized coding tasks, conducting deeper research, and writing quality.” The company shared some examples today:

Memory efficiency: A team of Argon agents analyzed fleet-wide profiling telemetry to autonomously identify and apply memory optimizations across Google’s data centers, freeing up over 300 TiB of memory once rolled out, with an estimated 500 TiB to 1 PiB in total savings.

Large Scale Codebase Migrations and Optimizations: Argon agents are working on migrating C/C++ codebases to Rust across Google—scaling from tens of thousands of lines in core libraries like re2, libgav1 up to 800K+ lines for the Fuchsia OS Zircon kernel. Given the criticality of many of these systems, such large-scale rewrites are undergoing rigorous automated and manual auditing, emulation testing, and review before rolling out to production.

For libgav1, Google’s open source software for decoding video, Argon agents took an existing Rust port and replaced 32K lines of SIMD code by running many rounds of profile-guided experiments, studying the compiler’s output, producing safe Rust so the compiler would vectorize it automatically. The end result is a memory-safe video decoder that runs 2.7x faster than the Rust port, with identical video output, bringing it closer to the optimized C++.
