title: Apple Music 7.0 beta brings Liquid Glass redesign to Android
snippet: Apple Music for Android is getting a big Liquid Glass-inspired redesign with the latest 7.0 beta. more…
fullText:
Apple Music for Android is getting a big Liquid Glass-inspired redesign with the latest 7.0 beta.

With Liquid Glass now a year old on Apple platforms, the new design language is coming to Android. Apple Music now has a floating bottom bar that lets you see what is above, below, and to the sides. The navigation element has a small amount of translucency that allows you to mostly see solid colors underneath.

Old vs. new

Similarly, the mini-player above it gets the same treatment and is no longer docked with the bottom bar. Compared to Liquid Glass on iOS, scrolling does not collapse the bar into a more compact version, with everything remaining in place.

	

Top bars across the app have been updated, with the page title and overflow menu on the same line. The three-dot icons are no longer themed red and have been placed in circular containers. The Library tab sees the biggest update with “Edit Pins” and “Edit Categories” now part of the overflow.

Artist pages get a big update with the background now themed based on the cover image. This closely matches the iOS design with a more prominent play button and info page that’s no longer at the very bottom. Share has also been placed in the top-right corner.

The Settings page has also been modernized with better grouping. There are no major changes to Now Playing, which did not see any big updates on iOS.

Finally, Apple Music 7.0 now has an edge-to-edge design for the status and navigation bars.

With the last release, Apple Music for Android switched to a new versioning system that aligns with iOS. Today’s version 7.0 aligns with iOS 27.

Apple Music 7.0 is currently in beta, with testing usually lasting a few weeks. You can sign up from the Play Store listing or this page. In general, these builds are fairly stable.

title: The clever way Apple embedded Face ID beneath the iPhone 18 Pro screen
snippet: In the iPhone 18 Pro, Apple has taken one of the next steps toward its long-term vision of the iPhone as a single slab of glass: embedding the Face ID module beneath the display. Achieving this without having the Face ID array be visible through the display and without compromising the quality of this section of the screen required some clever engineering … more…
fullText:
In the iPhone 18 Pro, Apple has taken one of the next steps toward its long-term vision of the iPhone as a single slab of glass: embedding the Face ID module beneath the display.

Achieving this without having the Face ID array be visible through the display and without compromising the quality of this section of the screen required some clever engineering …

Jony Ive described his long-term vision of the iPhone design as a single slab of glass, and while he is no longer with the company, that goal has remained. Eventually, Apple wants to embed all of the technology requiring screen real estate beneath the display, including both Face ID and front-facing camera.

The iPhone 18 Pro has achieved the first of these, but it was no easy task. Face ID requires infrared light to be both emitted and received by the TrueDepth module – and IR light cannot pass through display pixels.

Apple needed to create gaps between the pixels large enough to allow the IR light to pass between them, but without any visible degradation in the display. To do so, the company’s engineers set out to design a different pixel layout with larger gaps without visibly impacting what can be displayed on those pixels. 

iFixit used a microscope to show this pixel pattern, with Apple confirming to me me that the overall pixel density over the module is reduced by half. This would potentially have created a second problem: half the pixel density might have created a visibly dimmer section of the display, so Apple increases the brightness of these pixels to compensate. There also appears to be an IR pass filter to block visible light from passing through the gaps, further hiding the components.

The result is remarkable. For all practical purposes, the TrueDepth camera array is impossible to see even when staring at it extremely closely. I couldn’t capture it even using macro photography with different screen colors and lighting conditions. That’s not to say it’s completely impossible to detect, as iFixit’s microscope view shows, but rather that there is absolutely no way you’ll notice it in everyday use.

Right now, that achievement reduces the size of the Dynamic Island, which in turn enables support for three live activities rather than two. In some future iPhone model, the front-facing camera will also be hidden beneath the display. That’s technically possible today, but the compromise in image quality is currently greater than Apple is willing to accept. Solving that issue is a matter of when rather than if.

title: Google Photos rolling out Redact tool, Mood filters, & more
snippet: Google Photos is rolling out a handful of new features, including a Redact Markup tool and “Moods” on Android. more…
fullText:
Google Photos is rolling out a handful of new features, including a Redact Markup tool and “Moods” on Android.

The upgraded Markup tool adds three features, starting with a Redact pen that lets you blur/pixelate sensitive info in screenshots and images. There are also precise thickness sliders for the Pen and new fonts in the Text tool. This is rolling out globally to Google Photos for Android.

Moods let you easily apply a “nostalgic, vintage-inspired look” to pictures, including Crisp 35mm (film), 2000’s night (digicam), Retro contrast, Night light, Blue Haze, Any Minimalist, and Rich textures. You get slider controls, with each mood “intelligently adapt[ing] to your images.” This is rolling out globally on Android.

There are also 15 new Remix templates, including red carpet moments, whimsical birthday cards, and photo booth shots. This is rolling out in select countries on Android and iOS.

	

Google Photos is also highlighting how the Wardrobe feature is now available in Brazil, India, and the US on Android and iOS. An AI Pro or AI Ultra subscription is required. There’s also the Photos integration in Gemini Spark announced earlier this month.

“Carême” follows the thrilling story of the world’s first celebrity chef, Antonin Carême (Voisin), who rose from humble beginnings in Paris to the height of culinary stardom in Napoleon’s Europe. While he dreams only of becoming the most famous chef in the world, his talent and ambitions attract the attention of renowned and powerful politicians who use him as a spy for France. Determined to escape poverty and fulfill his dream, Carême can choose revenge or he can have it all — women, wealth, fame — but at what cost? His love? His soul? His life?

iPhone Duo pre-orders start on Friday, October 16, but Apple just announced when you can get an early start on the process. Here are the details.

Apple will let you ‘Get ready’ for iPhone Duo pre-orders beginning October 12 for fastest checkout

When Apple launches a major new iPhone model, it usually offers a window of time during which you can ‘Get ready’ for the pre-order by making your selections in advance.

The company just confirmed it will do the same for iPhone Duo. Per a new update on Apple’s website, you can begin the iPhone Duo pre-order process as early as Monday, October 12.

Starting October 12, and likely running through much of the day October 15, you’ll be able to go to the Apple Store app or Apple’s online store and make your pre-order selections in advance.

By completing this process ahead of time, Apple says you can get through checkout faster when iPhone Duo pre-orders go live on Friday, October 16 at 8:00 a.m. ET / 5:00 a.m. PT.

If you haven’t done it before, I highly recommend the ‘Get ready’ process to anyone ordering directly from Apple. It’s a great way to minimize potential hiccups on the morning of pre-orders, which means you’ll have a better chance of launch day delivery.

title: Honor Magic 9 Pro Max goes official with 8,800 mAh battery, ARRI cameras, Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6
snippet: Honor has officially announced its latest flagship in China, with the Honor Magic 9 Pro Max packing powerful specs, upgraded cameras, the latest Snapdragon chip, and confirmed for an global launch later on. more…
fullText:
Honor has officially announced its latest flagship in China, with the Honor Magic 9 Pro Max packing powerful specs, upgraded cameras, the latest Snapdragon chip, and confirmed for an global launch later on.

The Honor Magic 9 Pro Max is an all-out flagship with a heavy focus on its cameras, so let’s start there.

Continuing its ARRI partnership that debuted on the Robot Phone, the Magic 9 Pro Max packs a 200MP main camera with “gimbal-level stabilization,” a 200MP telephoto camera with 3.5x optical zoom, and a 50MP ultra-wide camera. Those are arranged on the back in the style of an ARRI cinema camera, and they’re also tuned by ARRI to produce better colors both in photos and videos. Honor is also building out additional hardware including two teleconverter lenses and a “Mobile Video Kit” in partnership with SmallRig.

The front-facing camera is no slouch either, with a 55MP sensor that’s paired with a 3D depth sensing camera for face unlock.

	

The phone surrounding those cameras packs a punch too. 

Honor Magic 9 Pro Max is powered by the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 and starts at 12GB of RAM and 256GB of storage. Honor is using its own “Imaging Chip H1” to enhance camera processing, with MagicOS 11 based on Android 17 also available out of the box (with all its Liquid Glass-y-ness). The display is a 6.8-inch 2868×1320 OLED panel with Honor’s NanoCrystal Shield on top (which is both anti-scratch and anti-reflective), 10,000 nits of peak brightness – somehow –, 1-120Hz adaptive refresh rate support, and a 4,320Hz PWM dimming rate for better eye comfort. There’s an 8,800 mAh battery inside with 100W wired charging and 80W wireless, and the whole phone has IP68, IP69, and IP69K dust/water resistance ratings. 

Honor Magic 9 Pro Max specs

6.8-inch 2868×1320 LTPO OLED display, NanoCrystal glass, 4,320Hz PWM, 10,000 nits peak brightness

Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6

12/256GB, 12/512GB, 16/512GB, 16/1TB

MagicOS 11 based on Android 17

Rear Cameras: 200MP main (f/1.57), 200MP telephoto (f/2.6, 3.5x optical zoom, up to 200x digital zoom), 50MP ultrawide with autofocus

Front Camera: 55MP + 3D depth-sensing camera

8,800 mAh battery, 100W wired charging, 80W wireless charging

IP68/IP69/IP69K

The Magic 9 Pro Max is available today in China, but Honor says global availability is coming soon. Europe, MEA (Middle East & Africa), SEA (Southeast Asia), and “other key international markets” are all confirmed at this point, but there’s no reason to expect this one in the US. 

Honor also launched the Magic 9 in China.

It has a similar design but with a smaller 6.37-inch display, Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, a very similar camera array, and an 8,000 mAh battery.

title: John Ternus has big plans to make Apple ‘leaner’ and release more products
snippet: New CEO John Ternus has plans to “overhaul” Apple in an attempt to make it “run faster and leaner,” according to a new report from Bloomberg. This includes introducing more products, eliminating “middle-management positions,” and much more. more…
fullText:
New CEO John Ternus has plans to “overhaul” Apple in an attempt to make it “run faster and leaner,” according to a new report from Bloomberg. This includes introducing more products, eliminating “middle-management positions,” and much more.

John Ternus wants to reshape Apple, here’s how

First, the new Apple CEO wants to release more products faster than before, including becoming “more experimental.” One idea is to shake up Apple’s release calendar and rely less on the typical spring-and-fall cadence, instead releasing more new products throughout the year. 

Ternus also wants to “create a leaner organization with a greater focus on engineering.” This includes several cost-cutting measures and restructuring. For instance, one change is “eliminating some middle-management positions to reduce the layers separating engineers from senior executives.”

The report says Apple has dismissed “a number of engineering program managers, or EPMs,” in its hardware engineering division over the last two weeks. Bloomberg describes these roles as having been “central to Apple’s product-development process for decades,” responsible for “managing timelines and coordinating work across teams.”

“The cuts affected several program managers, including roughly half a dozen directors, one of the company’s most senior employee levels,” the report says. “Those employees were given just weeks to find other positions within Apple. Those who don’t secure new roles will be laid off later this year.”

Bloomberg says the cost-cutting measures could go much broader than that, though. Ternus has reportedly advocated for Apple to be “leaner” for years:

Ternus, 51, has advocated for a leaner organization for years. While leading hardware engineering, he told employees during an all-hands meeting that Apple should hire fewer people, ask more of its existing engineers and reduce organizational bloat. During a presentation, he showed a slide charting annual headcount growth and argued that the company should be accomplishing more with fewer employees.

Furthermore, Apple reportedly scrapped a plan over the summer to lay off 5,000 AppleCare employees, believing that AI-powered agents could handle those responsibilities.

At the same time, Ternus wants Apple to increase revenue from Apple’s services division alongside Eddy Cue and CFO Kevan Parekh. “They have discussed launching new services and extracting more revenue from existing products and offerings,” the report says.

Ultimately, one source told Bloomberg that things are “hectic” inside Apple right now:

“Everything is a lot more hands-on than it used to be,” said one person familiar with the situation. “It’s hectic right now.” That person and others said managers in product-development groups are being pushed to deliver more products, more frequently and on shorter timelines.

You can read the full report at Bloomberg. It’s a fascinating piece that I highly recommend reading in full.

title: iOS 27 brings three key new features to Find My
snippet: iOS 27 brings new features to almost all of Apple’s apps, including Messages, Apple Music, Wallet, and more. Apple’s Find My app has its own share of changes in iOS 27. Here’s everything new. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 brings new features to almost all of Apple’s apps, including Messages, Apple Music, Wallet, and more. Apple’s Find My app has its own share of changes in iOS 27. Here’s everything new.

iOS 27: What’s new for Find My?

Apple touts three changes to Find My in iOS 27:

More flexible sharing options

UI enhancements

Apple Watch updates

First, more flexible sharing options in Find My give you more control over when and for how long you share your location with others. “Share your location for a custom duration or until a set date and time,” Apple says. You can also now “pause sharing with people individually, whenever you want.”

One of the bigger changes here is that you can now hide your location from a specific person without sending them any notification or alert. The other person won’t be notified when you pause, stop, or resume sharing your location with them.

Previously, you could turn off your location in the Find My app altogether, which wouldn’t send a notification. This, however, hid your location from everyone. In iOS 27, you can disable your location for specific people. 

To manage this, you’ll see a new “Hide Location” toggle on each person’s card in the Find My app. If you pause sharing your location with someone, they will see a “No Location Found” message in their Find My app.

Design changes

As for the UI enhancements, Find My in iOS 27 has been refreshed with a new Liquid Glass interface. The app largely missed out on Liquid Glass in iOS 26, but this year it has a new tab bar design that matches Apple’s other apps.

The Find My interface now also shows more specific location information on the app’s main page. This means you don’t have to tap on each person to view exactly what street they’re on at any given moment.

There is also new iconography in the Find My app in iOS 27. The “Items” tab, for example, is now denoted by a new AirTag-style icon.

Apple Watch updates

Finally, for cellular Apple Watch users, sharing your location will automatically use your Apple Watch when you’re away from your iPhone or iPad. 

Also on Apple Watch, there’s a redesigned, unified Find My app that integrates people, items, and devices into one interface.

title: iPhone video stabilization continues to wow me in the iPhone 18 Pro
snippet: I first talked about how much iPhone video stabilization impressed me when I tested it on the iPhone 13 Pro back in 2021. It’s been improved significantly since then, with both the iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro having a version Apple refers to as “ultra-stabilized video.” While it doesn’t sound as sexy as some features, it makes a massive difference to the usability of the iPhone for handheld shooting – and my latest test really drove home just how good it is today … more…
fullText:
I first talked about how much iPhone video stabilization impressed me when I tested it on the iPhone 13 Pro back in 2021. It’s been improved significantly since then, with both the iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro having a version Apple refers to as “ultra-stabilized video.”

While it doesn’t sound as sexy as some features, it makes a massive difference to the usability of the iPhone for handheld shooting – and my latest test really drove home just how good it is today … 

I have a mini tripod and GorillaPod that I carry with me when I know I’m going to want to shoot some iPhone video footage, but of course, one of the huge benefits of an iPhone is that it’s the camera you always have with you. There are times when I spot an opportunity for a shot and don’t have a tripod with me. 

It’s often possible to improvise, whether that’s by leaning the iPhone against a railing or bracing myself against something like a lamppost. But there are times when I rely on the built-in video stabilization on iPhones, and in the most recent example, shooting with the iPhone 18 Pro, I was incredibly impressed. 

A riverboat trip down the Thames demonstrated that there are times when the iPhone’s built-in video stabilization feature is actually better than a tripod. That’s because the boat rocks around a fair bit, which would have meant a stable shot of the boat with the scenery outside moving around. The iPhone reliably stabilized to the outside world with the boat moving around in the foreground.

That ability to keep the horizon true no matter what movements the platform makes is something we don’t even get with a typical gimbal. Most consumer-grade ones smooth out movement rather than eliminating it. It’s only with high-end professional gimbals and the type of giro mount designed for marine and helicopter use that we get truly locked horizons.

The iPhone 18 Pro’s ultra-stabilization feature honestly delivers this level of performance, and that’s a pretty incredible feature to have as standard in the stock Camera app with no external hardware required.

Check out the sample footage below. If you don’t want to take the full ride, the Tower Bridge section starting here is probably the best showcase for the feature. But if you do want to enjoy the London tourist experience, hit C to switch on the captions for all the bridge names and a few other comments, including pointing out Apple’s UK campus.

fullText:
Good morning. Today I’m going crazy over the NYT’s list of the best TV shows of the 21st century, redoing all of my vibe-projects with Opus 5.5, girding my loins for another Witcher 3 play-through now that the free remaster is out, and devouring Colson Whitehead’s new novel, Cool Machine.

As a reminder, Inbox is the tech newsletter that goes beyond the news cycle. We cover the most important 9to5Google stories from the last couple of days along with a few highlights from around the web. We publish every Tuesday and Thursday, and if you like what you read, please subscribe.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

⭐️ Starred

October 4th marks 10 years since Google debuted the Pixel, and over the next few days we plan to dive into the brand’s storied legacy. What started with a couple of HTC-built devices has expanded into an ecosystem that includes budget and flagship smartphones, smartwatches, earbuds, tablets, and more. 

	

The Pixel has served several purposes for Google throughout its lifespan, beginning as an extension of Nexus’s “Android best practices” before morphing into something a bit more complicated and abstract. When it debuted, Google emphasized the Pixel’s camera advantages, of which there were many, along with timely annual platform updates that arrived months before other Android devices.

As time went on, the Pixel brand came to encompass more than just smartphones; the company debuted its Tensor SoC inside the Pixel 6, and expanded the line to include the Pixel Watch, Pixel Buds, and a couple of failed Pixel-branded tablets. 

Perhaps the most remarkable thing about the Pixel lineup is its longevity; under Rick Osterloh, the brand has become synonymous with deep integration into Google’s services — of late, particularly Gemini — and a steward of thoughtful software and hardware design. The company’s products have made inroads in many markets, but still represent a single-digit share in most, including the US (despite solid year-over-year growth in 2026).

It’s perhaps also worth pointing out that the Pixel lineup has persevered in spite of many challenges, from major hardware issues with the Pixel 2 and 3 series to Covid-related supply constraints in the Pixel 5 to reputation-harming modem performance in the Pixel 6. It really wasn’t until 2023’s Pixel 8 series that Google shook its image as a mediocre hardware vendor and married superlative hardware with delightful software.

Today, the Pixel lineup is both the best and most predictable it’s ever been. The Pixel 11 series is yet another iteration on a design that debuted in 2021 with the Pixel 6. The Pixel Watch has looked identical since its 2022 debut. The Pixel Buds are fine but not competitive. The Pixel Tablet appears to be dead, and there’s no sign of a Pixelbook successor on the horizon.

Ten years in, is the Pixel brand where Google wanted it to be, with its cultural influence outpacing its financial viability? Perhaps not, but it’s also not likely to disappear anytime soon, which speaks volumes about its importance, both to the company and the community that keeps it in the conversation.

✉️ Inbox

🤝 Cc: Max Weinbach

Welcome to Cc:, where I ask interesting people in the community about what’s making them happy both inside and outside the world of tech. This week, I’m speaking with Max Weinbach, who used to contribute to 9to5Google and is now a tech analyst with Creative Strategies.

Who are you?

I’m Max Weinbach, an analyst at Creative Strategies. You might also know me from writing about phones at XDA and 9to5Google, or from spending way too much time talking about technology on Twitter.

What do you do for work?

I research and write about consumer technology, especially phones, PCs, chips, and AI. A lot of my work now is figuring out what AI can actually do when you give it a real task, real data, and the tools to finish the job. I also consider my job to be just knowing a lot about many different technology topics. 

That has turned into building things, too. We’ve been working on Diligence Stack and practical agent benchmarks, testing how the model, the tools, and the surrounding software affect the result. I want to know whether something can produce useful work and how much fixing it needs afterward. That tells me a lot more than a score by itself.

What do you do for fun?

I build things and play games. There’s quite a bit of overlap between my hobbies and my work. I’ll get interested in some software problem and end up with another side project. I’ve been spending a lot of time on native apps and experimenting with AI agents.

Reviewing gaming hardware is also a very convenient excuse to play something I’ve been putting off. That’s how I finally got around to Alan Wake 2 and picked Spider-Man 2 back up. 

On top of that, the classics of harassing playing with my dog and going to the gym. I’ve spent a lot of time learning about health and wellness. It’s just interesting to learn about and put into practice for me!

What is your relationship like with technology these days?

I’m still excited about it, but I care a lot about the experience of actually using something. A great spec sheet only gets you so far if the laptop is annoying, the software gets in your way, or the AI needs more supervision than the task was worth.

Some of my favorite products are the ones that are almost boring because they get the basics right. A comfortable laptop that runs the things I need, lasts a long time, and doesn’t have some weird deal-breaking issue is genuinely exciting to me. I’m also interested in how much easier it’s becoming to build the software I want to use.

What are three apps you can’t live without and why?

ChatGPT. I love ChatGPT as a product. It’s one of those apps that just let me kinda delegate whatever I want, and it will simply do it. It’s good for research, good for building one-off apps here and there, and just a great platform to help with anything I can think of. It doesn’t replace any actual work for me, but makes that work much easier and quicker. 

Whoop. Technically, an app and a product, but the product powers the app so I’m going with it. It’s one of my favorite ways to track health and wellness because it’s the first that has basically nailed the feeling of recovery and strain on a daily basis. In the morning I actually try to guess what the number will be based on what I feel, and I get it pretty close every morning. 

X/Twitter. X is one of my favorite ways to actually consume media and news, share my thoughts, keep up with friends. Yes, I know this is such a normal choice and nothing unique here, but I don’t know, I really like the app. My life would be very different without it.

What is a gadget that you love right now?

Plaud’s Note Pro MagSafe thing. It’s fantastic, and makes my life significantly easier all around when it comes to notes. I tend to have a good memory when it comes to meetings, so I tend to not take notes. That only gets you so far when it comes to specific details, and I find actually writing notes distracting. This thing solves it for me: take a recording, transcribe, and generate key notes while I can listen. Yes, voice memos exist on every phone and watch but I like this a lot more.

How does AI fit into your life right now?

It’s a big part of how I build and research things. I use agents for coding, testing ideas, and working through problems, then look at what they actually produce. The useful question for me is how close they get to a result I can use.

One recent example is having agents write and optimize Metal kernels for a local model, testing changes on the hardware as they go. I still choose between cloud and local models based on the job. Having the option to use both is valuable. 

I also have a ton of little ideas of how things should work, apps I want, little fun animations or widgets or whatever I can think of for my different products or phones or connecting to Siri and I can just make it by dictating into a magic box and an hour later it’s installed on my products.

What is a recent TV show you loved?

Lanterns, I think it’s just a fun good show that, while it’s not done yet, is just fun. It’s a superhero show that’s not a superhero show entirely. It’s simply a great story told extremely well with characters I like.

What is a recent game you loved?

Marvel’s Spider-Man 2. I bought a PS5 to play it and then never finished it, so reviewing the MSI Claw gave me a good excuse to start again. It looks fantastic, and the movement and combat work really well on a controller. I ended up getting into the game rather than constantly thinking about the hardware. When the testing was done, I kept playing.

What is something offline you do every day that brings you joy?

Spending time with Malibu, my Goldendoodle. It’s a good reason to put the computer down for a bit. Otherwise, I enjoy being online. It’s a good way to connect with the world and what interests me. I know a lot of people want to disconnect because the world is stressful, but that’s reality and I like it. I’d rather absorb it all and just make using technology, or being online, a normal thing rather than seeing it as this overarching bad thing that is ruining lives.

🗑️ Trash

Samsung sells a lot of refrigerators. But as reported by Ars Technica (via Star News Korea), a failed firmware update caused some Korean owners’ fridges to “suddenly [lose] power and stop functioning.”

The unfortunate situation occurred right before the Korean holiday of Chuseok, so fridges were likely stocked full of perishables. Samsung said that it immediately halted the firmware update and was “taking emergency measures” on behalf of affected customers.

This is why we can’t have nice things… like dumb fridges that don’t require software updates.

title: Duo-Man turns your 2026 iPhone Duo into a 1980s Sony Walkman
snippet: Long before the iPod, the Sony Walkman was the device of choice for those who wanted to add a soundtrack to their life. Now a Duo-Man app recreates the experience for those of us old enough to have owned one, and you’ll be able to use it with Apple Music … more…
fullText:
Long before the iPod, the Sony Walkman was the device of choice for those who wanted to add a soundtrack to their life. Now a Duo-Man app recreates the experience for those of us old enough to have owned one, and you’ll be able to use it with Apple Music …

Prior to the Walkman, if you wanted to listen to music on the move, your options were limited. Most cassette players of the time were heavy and bulky. When Sony took an audio recorder designed for journalists and shrunk it into the smallest possible cassette player, it quickly became an iconic product.

Developer Vidit Bhargava created the app at a hackathon – and given that many of those present would never have seen one, he brought along the real thing to show them what it looked like.

Duo-Man offers the complete walkman experience on the iPhone Duo. Open the Duo to pick and 'insert' the cassette, Close the Duo to start listening.

Yes, I actually recorded the button clicks and static noise from a real Walkman!

It was fun making this at @bitrig hacks today. pic.twitter.com/juSrLhofrH

— Vidit Bhargava (@viditb) September 27, 2026

You open the Duo, choose your album to insert the tape, and then close it to play.

Bhargava said he originally only created it as a demo app for fun, but will now be releasing it as an actual app. The best comment in the X thread is this one, an image that will only make sense to people of a certain age.

title: Google Messages finally rolls out new long-press menu with precise copying
snippet: After testing got underway in January, Google Messages is finally widely rolling out a new long-press menu in conversations. more…
fullText:
After testing got underway in January, Google Messages is finally widely rolling out a new long-press menu in conversations.

This new design replaces the top toolbar that housed various actions. Google only surfaced three actions with everything else in an overflow menu.

	

Upon long-pressing on a chat message or image, Google will show a floating menu with Remix (photos), Reply, Forward, Copy (text), Star, Delete, Select more, Info, and Save (photos).

Each action is accompanied by an icon at the front for quick scanning, while Copy lets you highlight a specific part of the message by pressing down and dragging the bubble. Previously, you could only copy the entire message.

	

If you’ve selected the newest message in a thread, Google will somewhat center it with a bouncy animation and haptic feedback. Messages prominently blurs the background layer when this menu is active. The row of emoji and “Create” Photomoji shortcuts is unchanged.

As of today, we’re seeing the new Google Messages long-press menu widely rolled out with stable version 20260910_03_RC02. There is a server-side component, so be sure to Force stop from the App info menu if it’s not yet live.

title: Motorola’s wide Galaxy Z Fold 8 competitor might be very tiny and called ‘Razr Flex’
snippet: According to a new leak, Motorola’s upcoming entry in the wide, book-style foldable space may be called “Razr Flex” and pack some very familiar specs. more…
fullText:
According to a new leak, Motorola’s upcoming entry in the wide, book-style foldable space may be called “Razr Flex” and pack some very familiar specs.

Specs for Motorola’s wide foldable were shared by Android Headlines alongside a possible name for the device – “Razr Flex.” That’s apparently the name being used internally around the device, so it’s unclear if that would be used as a consumer-facing name. The codename is “Parker,” the report claims.

Much more interesting are the details around the side of this foldable, which shares the same general form factor as Samsung’s smash hit Galaxy Z Fold 8, just in a much smaller footprint. Apparently, the outer display is just 4.97-inches in size – the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is 5.5-inches – while the inner display is less than 7-inches across. Very tiny by modern phone standards, even in this new form factor.

The leaked specs include:

	

4.97-inch outer display (1736×1140)

6.92-inch inner display (2364×1728)

110x149x5.8mm unfolded | 110x76x12.6mm folded

215g

Snapdragon 8 Gen 5

12GB RAM

256GB of storage

5,000 mAh battery with Qi2 (magnets unclear)

IP48/49

50MP main/50MP ultrawide rear cameras, 32MP selfie cameras

PANTONE Coriander, PANTONE Dark Botanical Garden

It’s important to stress just how much smaller this is compared to other wide foldables. iPhone Duo is thicker and heavier than Samsung’s phone, but has roughly the same screen sizes. The closest comparison is the Xiaomi 18 Fold, which has a 5.38-inch outer display, but even that still has a 7.58-inch inner panel. 

The specs are otherwise pretty familiar to the full-size Razr Fold that launched earlier this year.

Concept renders were also shared, but they’re explicitly not based on, well, anything except sketches and Motorola’s general design language – take them not just with a grain of salt, but maybe a whole container.

The “Razr Flex” is said to be launching this year with a “mid-December” debut mentioned.

title: Pixel Buds app update lets Gemini control audio and settings
snippet: With the Pixel 11 launch, Google promised a big Pixel Buds update in September. We’re now starting to see Gemini audio controls with the latest Pixel Buds companion app update. more…
fullText:
With the Pixel 11 launch, Google promised a big Pixel Buds update in September. We’re now starting to see Gemini audio controls with the latest Pixel Buds companion app update.

After updating to version 1.0.981607934 of the Pixel Buds app, we’re seeing @Pixel Buds in Gemini as the latest Connected App. You can control “settings like EQ preset, ANC mode, conversation detection, and touch controls.”

Hey Google, turn up the bass

Hey Google, turn on noise cancellation

This brings up the Gemini overlay, with a “Connecting to Pixel Buds” message appearing along with verbal confirmation.

On devices without the app update, those commands just open the system Bluetooth settings page.

	

We’re seeing Pixel Buds 1.0.981607934 widely rolled out via the Play Store today.

The three other features Google previewed presumably require a firmware update. The Pixel Buds Pro 2 will get Dynamic ANC that adjusts to “compensate when subtle shifts in the seal happen,” like if the buds move in your ear. There’s also Pixel Watch sleep sync that pauses music, disables touch controls, and silences notifications on the Pixel Buds. Finally, you will be able to trigger Live translate by tapping your Pixel Buds.

title: Samsung’s open-ear Galaxy Buds On leak, showing what they look like when worn
snippet: Once rumored to go by a different name, Samsung’s Galaxy Buds On open-ear designs have appeared with a little more detail in new images, suggesting these earbuds might become official sooner rather than later. more…
fullText:
Once rumored to go by a different name, Samsung’s Galaxy Buds On open-ear designs have appeared with a little more detail in new images, suggesting these earbuds might become official sooner rather than later.

The Galaxy Buds On have been leaked several times over the last couple of months, though rumors suggested the earbuds would go by “Galaxy Buds Able” instead of the “Galaxy Buds On” name. That information was gleaned from Samsung’s Wearable app in early July, though the first of the two names seems to be an internal moniker.

New images of the Galaxy Buds On have surfaced (via Android Headlines). Previously, we’ve seen detailed renders and icon images, but nothing that looks like it could be official from Samsung. The new photos look a little cleaner, and one looks likely to be from the marketing team.

The Galaxy Buds On images also show what they look like when worn properly – that is, clipped around the ears rather than resting in them. It’s also a different style from the open-ear design worn over the ear. They look uncomfortable, but the design is already plentiful in certain regions, suggesting it’s a popular form factor.

	

It’s hard to pick up any details from the earbud images or to determine which port is the driver and which is the microphone for ambient noise detection. Even if that were determined properly, there’s no telling how they’ll sound prior to release.

The Galaxy Buds On were reported to have a few interesting features when previous images were leaked, such as an “Auto Volume” setting and head-nod and shake gesture control. Samsung Galaxy users will also have voice memos automatically transcribed to text.

Other devices like the Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra have been circulating alongside the Galaxy Buds On, suggesting Samsung is gearing up for another launch soon. When that is, there’s no telling right now.

In recent years, Macs had been getting more and more affordable. Cheaper starting points, more memory and storage per dollar, and the introduction of MacBook Neo. For the first time, Apple had started to become one of the best values on the market.

Unfortunately, Apple just drastically increased its prices because of the ongoing memory shortage. Macs aren’t as appealing as they were a few months ago, that said, there’s still some decent deals out there – and if you’re in need of a new computer, I’d still say todays Macs are a good value against the rest of the computing market.

MacBook Air

Up until the launch of MacBook Neo, the MacBook Air represented the entry point to Apple’s laptop lineup. Despite MacBook Neo making its value proposition slightly questionable, I’d still say MacBook Air is a great laptop if you want a better experience without needing anything premium.

MagSafe, a P3 color display, Center Stage on the webcam, and more battery life are just a few of the highlights with MacBook Air. It also comes with a 15-inch size variant, unlike MacBook Neo which only offers 13-inch.

title: The Googlebook marketing push starts with Henry Cavill and his mustache
snippet: Ahead of next month’s launch, Google is beginning the marketing push for Googlebooks with Henry Cavill. more…
fullText:
Ahead of next month’s launch, Google is beginning the marketing push for Googlebooks with Henry Cavill.

The company announced today that it partnered with actor and tech enthusiast Henry Cavill to “help showcase the potential of this next-generation laptop.” Google is specifically referring to “unique software experiences like Continue on phone syncing, Rambler speech-to-text, Antigravity and so much more.”

Cavill, who is a big PC gamer, uses an Android phone. He previously used Pixel phones, with the last appearing to be the Pixel 5, while he was most recently spotted with a Galaxy S25 Ultra.

Google is very much leaning into that: “We recently met with Henry to discuss his own creative ambitions and the conversation quickly turned to the need for a laptop that could keep up with him and work seamlessly with his Android phone.”

	

The premise of this marketing campaign is that Henry Cavill will use a Googlebook to “build a video game.” He’s seen using the HP Googlebook 14 today.

“When Google reached out to me and explained what they are doing with Googlebook, and all of its new, integrated tools, it had me intrigued. So, I asked for the opportunity to have a play with it ahead of release. After being hands on and spending some time with their team, I believe this has the potential to be the start of something rather special. Time and technology are marching forward at a breakneck pace, this, and all that Google are trying to do with it, has the whispers of the next generation.”

—Henry Cavill

This passion project will get underway in November, with @Android on Instagram providing updates, while there’s now a dedicated page: googlebook.google/henry-cavill.

More broadly, Google heavily advertising Googlebooks will be key to its success and this is definitely a start. Hopefully, this will be followed by traditional online and TV campaigns.

title: Reminders just got more powerful, here’s what’s new in iOS 27
snippet: iOS 27 adds new features to Apple Notes, Messages, Wallet, and more, and it has a few improvements for the Reminders app too. Here’s everything new for Reminders in iOS 27. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 adds new features to Apple Notes, Messages, Wallet, and more, and it has a few improvements for the Reminders app too. Here’s everything new for Reminders in iOS 27.

#1: Describe your reminder

Reminders has offered some level of natural language support for new reminders for a while. But in iOS 27, Apple Intelligence upgrades the feature.

When creating a new reminder, type everything out in natural language and when you type certain info, like a due date, the keyboard row will suggest adding that date to the reminder.

Some basic version of this was available before, but Apple Intelligence makes it more accurate and provides more options than before. Per Apple:

Describe a New Reminder: Use your own words to describe a reminder and Apple Intelligence will help create it for you.

This ‘Describe’ functionality now extends to the reminder detail screen too, letting you jot down your reminder and have it automatically adopt all of the relevant metadata you mention. 

Every time you add or edit reminders inside a list, iOS 27 upgrades the experience with more tools conveniently accessible than before.

In iOS 26, when creating or editing a task you would see five options above the keyboard row: Date, Location, Tag, Flag, and Camera.

In iOS 27, Reminders moves all metadata options into a new box that surrounds your active reminder. And it’s far more robust, with the new UI letting you modify the following:

Date

Time

Urgent

Repeat

Location

Tag

Flag

Camera

You can still tap the ‘i’ icon to view the full set of metadata options, but with iOS 27 you shouldn’t have to do that nearly as often.

#3: Grocery list improvements

Apple says that Reminders’ grocery list auto-sorting feature has been made better in two ways:

it now “sorts grocery list items more accurately”

and grocery list sorting expands to multiple languages

Essentially, due to the more powerful Foundation Models in iOS 27, this feature that’s been around a while is going to work better than ever.

More info on Reminders’ grocery list feature is available here.

title: Apple Watch Series 12 one week later: There’s so much more than meets the eye
snippet: When Apple unveiled the Apple Watch Series 12, two features stood out: the new Siri Recap feature, as well as the much improved heart rate monitor. While those two features were part of the reason I was compelled to buy the new Apple Watch, I’ve found myself delighted by much more than just those two things. more…
fullText:
When Apple unveiled the Apple Watch Series 12, two features stood out: the new Siri Recap feature, as well as the much improved heart rate monitor. While those two features were part of the reason I was compelled to buy the new Apple Watch, I’ve found myself delighted by much more than just those two things.

Battery and charging

While Apple’s website doesn’t quote any additional battery life for Apple Watch Series 12 compared to Series 11, the battery certainly feels like it lasts longer. As I’ve written in the past, I was someone who used the WHOOP prior to the Apple Watch Series 12, and even though I kept my Apple Watch, I never used it for sleep tracking.

After the keynote, I decided to give Apple Watch sleep tracking a shot. That said, on my Series 11, juggling sleep tracking and charging was a bit of a pain. After using the watch throughout the day, I’d have to charge it a little bit before going to sleep, then when I wake up, I’d have to charge it again.

On Series 12, that isn’t the case. It has enough battery to last through a day and overnight, and now I just charge it when I wake up. Apple Watch Series 12 also charges significantly faster, which makes that part less of a pain. 15 minutes of charging gets you up to 12 hours of use, per Apple.

I imagine the new S11 chip, derived from the A20 Pro’s 2nm design, is a large part of the reason why battery life feels so much longer. Regardless of the why, it feels amazing to not have charging anxiety around sleep tracking on the Apple Watch Series 12. Another big upside to the S11 chip? Apple Watch Series 12 feels so much faster, especially with Siri.

Software exclusives

On Series 12, Apple finally includes a proper step counter as a complication, which I like checking on in my smart stack. Could this come to older Apple Watches? Probably. It’s not like Apple didn’t count steps before. Apple Watch Series 12 certainly counts them more accurately, but given the fact that the data is there, I think Apple should just add the complication. Either way, it’s nice to have on Series 12.

Another neat new feature is the entire Readiness app, which gives you an idea of how okay you’re doing today based on last night’s sleep, your previous day’s activity, and your vitals. This is similar to a recovery score on WHOOP, and I was certainly happy to see Apple add this to the Apple Watch? It’s a bit of a bummer it’s exclusive to the Series 12, but I could understand why Apple isn’t willing to calculate it with less accurate data.

Wrap up

All in all, the Apple Watch Series 12 is a rather nice upgrade. It’s a total S year, but if you care about your Apple Watch actually doing more rather than just looking different, I’d say this might be one of the most substantial year over year upgrades since Apple Watch Series 4.

The bezels certainly got a slight bit thicker compared to Series 10 and 11. As someone who uses a watch face with a black background, I can’t say I’ve noticed this much – though I hope Apple improves on this in the next iteration.

One last thing of note: Apple Watch Series 12 offers Ceramic Shield 2 on the aluminum models, making it hold up to scratches much better than older Apple Watch models. I haven’t owned mine long enough to truly test this, though so far my Apple Watch still looks perfect.

title: Big Tech Meets Death in a Hilarious Anti-Enshittification Ad
snippet: Cory Doctorow and a Norwegian nonprofit are behind a comically dark campaign about how everything’s getting worse.
fullText:
Imagine, if you will, a pale figure of Death, dressed in a black robe holding a scythe, alongside a handsome, lumberjack-looking Nordic fella who goes by the name Enshittificator. As partners in crime, they conspire to make your life suck, all because they have the power to make digital products and services worse. 

If that piques your interest — and maybe sounds too much like real life — a recent “anti-enshittification” ad campaign is worth a few minutes of your time.

The term “enshittification” was popularized in 2022 by author and activist Cory Doctorow, and its massive cultural surge earned it a place in Merriam-Webster’s slang hub last year. Enshittification is a deliberate process, designed by companies to maximize profit. 

			

More from CNET

It starts with luring you to a product or service, then making it so good that you become completely dependent on it. The next step is to pull the rug out from under you by hiding basic features behind a paywall, reducing overall quality and squeezing you for every last dime while providing as little value as possible. 

The Death and Enshittificator video above, released on YouTube in mid-September, is the second of a series from the Norwegian Consumer Council, an independent, government-funded nonprofit that advocates for consumer rights. The main character, the Enshittificator, is a bearded Nordic man who says in the first video, released in February, that his “job is to make things shitty.” 

The initial video concludes with Mr. Enshittificator getting into a car accident because he didn’t pay a subscription for his braking system, a scenario he appeared to find amusing. In the second video, he meets Death in the hospital, and the two enter into a business relationship. (He now dons a yellow hazmat suit to stay alive.) 

The duo spends time making every conceivable product worse, from TVs and toothbrushes to smartphone storage. They point out that products with long lifespans, like the famously indestructible Nokia 3310 — which makes a cameo appearance — only generate revenue once. If companies want a profitable business model, however, they have to use low-quality materials, ensure products can’t be fixed and stop issuing updates. 

“Look at all the companies that used to make solid products,” the Enshittificator said. “Where are they now?”

“Dead,” Death said, and they share a knowing smile. 

The Norwegian Consumer Council’s ads are part of its Breaking Free initiative, a multipronged policy approach to make technology work in favor of consumers, rather than against them. The campaign craftily relies on dark humor to detail how enshittification affects everyday life, from paid subscription models to planned obsolescence, which forces you to buy newer devices. 

“The term is often used about digital services that gradually become less useful and more commercial,” an NCC representative told CNET in an email. “But the same feeling applies more broadly: Products that break down too soon cannot be repaired or stop working because support disappears. People recognize the experience immediately.”

It’s true. The videos are also a strikingly accurate commentary on the dismal state of products and gadgets in the digital age. The NCC told CNET that more videos are on the way, but they can’t promise they’ll be in the same universe featuring the same characters. 

Doctorow himself collaborated with the nonprofit to help launch the series, which he’s immensely pleased with. In an email to CNET, he said, “The idea that firms’ market power means that they can worsen their offerings with impunity, combined with the minor license to vulgarity of my dirty little word, have proven a winning combination for helping people direct their anger in the right direction.”

Real life (and death)

It would not be shocking if there were actual boardrooms that looked like this.Norwegian Consumer Council

The enshittification process is relatable and real. In 2020, Apple agreed to pay up to $500 million to settle the landmark “batterygate” class action lawsuit over allegations that it secretly slowed down older iPhone models through software updates. Powerful tech companies have poured massive amounts of money into lobbying against right-to-repair laws, preventing customers from fixing their own devices when they break.  

“It’s really important that the products can’t be fixed,” said the Enshittificator. “It breaks, then it dies, so you have to buy a new one. And another one. And another one. And another one. And another one.”

“This way, we’re actually slowly killing the planet as well,” a smiling Death said, helpfully chiming in. 

The videos also satirize how digital services slowly degrade over time. In one scene, the Enshittificator tells an employee, “The 1,000 pictures of your deceased mother are mine, and you’re going to pay for them.” It’s a direct nod to Google Photos’ 2021 policy shift, which ended free unlimited storage and capped free accounts at 15GB, requiring users to get a subscription to keep already uploaded photos on the platform. 

Another scene takes a jab at automakers who sell you basic functionality as an add-on subscription service. 

“I don’t have any more money. You have me in the palm of your hand,” said the Enshittificator in a fake presentation about selling cars. “You can crush me. So what do you do? Updates. Radio? Premium feature. Heating? Premium feature. Now I have a shitty car, and I can’t afford a new one, but what I can afford is a small monthly payment!”

This is a reference to BMW’s controversial microtransaction model, where it tried to make heated seats and other in-car features part of a subscription plan. While intense consumer backlash forced the German automaker to walk back some of the “add-ons,” several features remain behind a paywall. Other brands have followed suit — Hyundai’s BlueLink and Kia Connect require paid plans to use remote start. For a period, both manufacturers even omitted the remote-start button from the physical key fob, completely blocking owners from using the feature for free.

Can it be fixed?

It’s important, though a little depressing, to imagine how much better life would be if companies actually invested money into making their products better, safer and longer-lasting — and not just more profitable for them. 

An NCC representative told CNET that public response to the ad campaign has been remarkable, with the latest video reaching millions of views in a few days. “What matters most to us, though, is not the views themselves, but that people engage with the reports and policy proposals behind the campaigns.”

In its Breaking Free: Pathways to a Fair Technological Future report, the NCC argues that major tech business models “are often fundamentally incompatible with consumer and human rights.” To dismantle the “walled gardens run by Big Tech feudalists” and end dependence on Big Tech, the nonprofit is pushing for policy reforms built around a three-pronged strategy based on democratic values and principles of openness. 

The first is interoperability, which would force platforms to interface with one another. This is already taking shape under the EU’s Digital Markets Act, which required Apple to allow third-party app stores and mandated Meta to support external chats in WhatsApp, 

Next comes portability, which would allow users to move their contacts, content, photos and anything else to rival services. A subscriber fed up with Spotify adding AI features, for instance, would be able to switch to YouTube Music or Apple Music without losing their saved playlists, thereby eliminating platform lock-in. 

Arguably, the most difficult to implement is decentralization of social media, which could shift social media away from single-entity corporate control toward open networks like the Fediverse (which powers platforms such as Mastodon). Though still evolving as protocols develop, decentralization enhances interoperability, making cross-network movement frictionless.

The NCC also told CNET that there are immediate actions Norway (and other countries) can take, such as lowering the VAT (value-added tax) on repair materials, extending consumer claim periods and holding international e-commerce platforms to the same regulatory standards as local businesses.

Reining in Big Tech remains an uphill battle, but in the meantime, the campaign offers a hilarious — and painfully accurate — look at the modern digital hellscape.

“The true mark of success for a project like this is when other people pick it up and run with it,” Doctorow said.

title: Nothing Headphone (1) Pro are $399 with better hardware, ANC, and audio upgrades
snippet: Nothing is today introducing its new Headphone (1) Pro over-ear headphones which deliver hardware improvements, better ANC, and deeper control over how you can tune the final output. more…
fullText:
Nothing is today introducing its new Headphone (1) Pro over-ear headphones which deliver hardware improvements, better ANC, and deeper control over how you can tune the final output.

Following up on last year’s Nothing Headphone (1), the new Pro model brings upgrades across the board. That includes the physical hardware, which is a tiny bit lighter at 327g, while also getting softer ear cups, a wider headband, and thicker padding throughout. The design is also updated with a cleaner look and subtler accents, as well as glass in place of the previous plastic portions.

The biggest upgrades here are the ones that power the audio, though.

Nothing Headphone (1) Pro gets a triple-driver design that provides not only better audio quality, but far more control and flexibility throughout the tuning. In the Nothing X app you get a more advanced custom EQ interface with the option to independently adjust the main drivers and the third “precision driver.” You can get into the weeds of every little detail of the audio here, and it’s far more advanced even compared to the rest of Nothing’s audio gear.

	

Nothing built out the audio experience here with the help of Metropolis Studios, and Headphone (1) Pro also offers a physical switch to let you quickly jump to a “Flat” EQ for a completely neutral sound profile. There are also several presets for Spatial Audio that simulate listening locations such as “Live House,” “Concert Hall,” and more, with head tracking optional.

Active Noise Cancellation is also boosted here, hitting 46 dB, up from the 42 dB on Headphone (1). Nothing says this is through a 10-mic system and a stronger sound seal from the new earcups. 

Like on Headphone (1), Pro supports lossless audio over USB-C while supporting Hi-Res wireless playback as well. You also still get the same plethora of physical controls across the side including the paddle and wheel. 

I’ve been using Nothing Headphone (1) Pro for a few days and, while it’s too early to make a full verdict, there are meaningful improvements throughout, including the much more comfortable hardware. title: MagSafe Monday: Pioneer joins the MagSafe accessory market with the SDA-SC600
snippet: The Pioneer brand is one I’ve trusted for car accessories since Y2K was a concern. I loved their audio gear in my younger days. Pioneer’s SDA-SC600 aims to bring that kind of trusted quality to a MagSafe car mount, bringing Qi2 wireless charging and a built-in fan. more…
fullText:
The Pioneer brand is one I’ve trusted for car accessories since Y2K was a concern. I loved their audio gear in my younger days. Pioneer’s SDA-SC600 aims to bring that kind of trusted quality to a MagSafe car mount, bringing Qi2 wireless charging and a built-in fan.

MagSafe Monday: Every Monday, Bradley Chambers looks at the latest and greatest in the MagSafe and wireless charging industry to help you get the most out of your Apple devices that support wireless charging.

Pioneer’s SDA-SC600 is a MagSafe air vent mount that holds your iPhone for maps, calls, Siri, etc, and Pioneer also includes a metal ring in the box so non-MagSafe iPhones and Android devices can still mount and use MagSafe technology .

The Pioneer SDA-SC600 is Qi2-compatible, which is almost the latest standard (Qi2.2). Car chargers have historically been one of the weaker links in the MagSafe ecosystem, often topping out well below what you’d get from a wired charger. Qi2 is what you need to ensure a GPS navigation device doesn’t drain faster than you can charge it.

The fan is key in hot climates

Fast MagSafe charging generates heat, which can pose a challenge depending on your climate. Especially right now, I get into my car on 95-degree days, and it’s blistering inside. Pioneer’s integrated cooling fan is built specifically to fight this heat, forcing a slower charge. If you live somewhere with real summers, this is essential for a MagSafe car charger. Pioneer also lists the SDA-SC600 as temperature-resistant more broadly, so it’s built to hold up in extreme cabin conditions at both ends of the weather extremes.

Pioneer also added subtle RGB lightning for as something to set itself apart from other chargers. In the box, you get the mount itself, the air vent adapter, the metal ring for non-MagSafe devices, and a USB-C to USB-C cable to power charger/

Wrap up on Pioneer SDA-SC600

Overall, the Pioneer SDA-SC600 is a solid option for a MagSafe car charger. The light is a nice touch. It supports modern speeds and the fan should keep it cool. The light is a nice touch at night as well.

You can pick up the new Pioneer SDA-SC600 from Amazon or directly from Pioneer.

title: Here’s what I’d like to see Apple do right in a screenless fitness tracker
snippet: Last week, Bloomberg reported that Apple is working on a screenless fitness tracker, akin to a WHOOP or Fitbit Air. As someone who’s used the WHOOP for the past 6 months, I do think its a great concept, though there are a few things I’d like to see Apple do better. more…
fullText:
Last week, Bloomberg reported that Apple is working on a screenless fitness tracker, akin to a WHOOP or Fitbit Air. As someone who’s used the WHOOP for the past 6 months, I do think its a great concept, though there are a few things I’d like to see Apple do better.

We don’t have many details on what Apple’s screenless fitness tracker will look like, as the product is relatively early in development. At the earliest, it would debut in 2028. Bloomberg describes it as a “thin fabric band with a sensor-equipped computing module.”

Earlier this year, WHOOP and Chase had a promo where you could get a discounted or free WHOOP if you had a Sapphire card, and I took advantage of that. Since then, I’ve been a WHOOP user – though I never went all in on it.

The reasoning for that was simple: automatic workout detection will never be perfect, and I found it annoying to have to pull out my phone to log a workout, whether that be beforehand or retroactively. With the Apple Watch, you can just start the workout on the screen, and the WHOOP will sync the times from Apple Health. This was the main reason I kept wearing my Apple Watch. 

For gym workouts, pulling out your phone might be fine, but for casual biking for long walks I’d rather not have to fiddle with my phone.

So, for Apple’s screenless fitness tracker, I’d love to see some sort of button and indicator LED that you can use for starting and stopping a workout. You’d still need to go on your phone later to categorize the workout, but I’d much rather do that than have to deal with it in the moment. Apple could also develop a classification model based on certain factors.

Wrap up

If Apple managed to develop a screenless fitness tracker that didn’t feel like a pain to use without a phone, I think it’d be quite compelling. The form factor has many advantages, including comfort, battery life, and the ability to wear it alongside a traditional watch.

	

Personally, after evaluating the WHOOP, I do think I prefer just having a smartwatch, even with the battery life disadvantages. I do understand wanting something screenless so its distraction-free, but personally I just enable Do Not Disturb on my watch.

What do you think about Apple working on a screenless fitness tracker? What pricepoint would it need to be for you to buy one? Let us know in the comments.

title: Big Pixel VIPs widget redesign starts rolling out
snippet: Following the version 2.0 update rolling out earlier this week, Google is now beginning to launch the Pixel VIPs widget redesign announced in the September Feature Drop. more…
fullText:
Following the version 2.0 update rolling out earlier this week, Google is now beginning to launch the Pixel VIPs widget redesign announced in the September Feature Drop.

Previously, the widget could be expanded to take up your entire screen. This redesign limits Pixel VIPs to two layouts.

The 5×1 layout shows just one row of your prioritized contacts (up to four) at a time with the ability to scroll for more. This view pairs circular profile avatars with just first names, rather than including surnames as before. The change results in a more consistent widget appearance.

Old vs. new

	

The 5×2 configuration is now the max size for the Pixel VIPs widget. Depending on the number of contacts, Google will display rectangular cards that feature pill-shaped buttons to quickly call or message.

Meanwhile, unread messages will result in a circular badge appearing in the top-right of the circular profile or the messaging icon, which would benefit from being a little bit more noticeable in the latter configuration.

This is rolling out via a server-side update that is not yet widely available. It’s only appearing on one of our Pixel devices today.

Version 2.0 rolled out earlier this week with a fullscreen design that replaces the bottom sheet approach. There are also some tweaks to the feed, while a dock at the bottom of the screen lets you quickly switch between your VIPs.

title: Bellroy’s leather Pixel 11 Pro case is a keeper
snippet: Like any sane capitalist, I love getting new stuff. But there’s something heartening about those new things settling into age, like a fecund garden becoming slightly unwieldy, or a pair of shoes getting more comfortable as you use them. Similarly, I’ve always enjoyed the way a well-made leather case ages as it weathers the trials and tribulations of everyday life. Traditionally called a patina, it’s the lived-in quality that a piece of leather inherits as it absorbs skin oils, scratches, and the unpredictability of weather. more…
fullText:
Like any sane capitalist, I love getting new stuff. But there’s something heartening about those new things settling into age, like a fecund garden becoming slightly unwieldy, or a pair of shoes getting more comfortable as you use them.

Similarly, I’ve always enjoyed the way a well-made leather case ages as it weathers the trials and tribulations of everyday life. Traditionally called a patina, it’s the lived-in quality that a piece of leather inherits as it absorbs skin oils, scratches, and the unpredictability of weather.

So it was when I put on the new “Red Ochre” variant of the leather Pixel 11 Pro XL case from Bellroy. The Melbourne-based company has long been an official Made by Google partner, which means it’s always among the first case manufacturers to unveil its wares each August.

I’ve had the case on my phone for just over three weeks now, and I look forward to picking it up each time. Bellroy’s leather is thin and rigid, and is treated to prevent wear, which means that it takes longer than, say, a piece of Horween leather from Nomad, to age. But it also means it will look new for longer. Barring a few minor scratches, the case has survived more than a few child-related drops with aplomb.

	
	

On the structure side, the leather is reinforced with a rigid plastic frame that protrudes a millimeter or so above the display, and is covered internally by a microfiber lining. Magnets are present on the back for PixelSnap compatibility, and the buttons are made from anodized aluminum, which gives them a satisfying tactility akin to the phone’s buttons themselves.

At $59, this is not a cheap case, but to my eyes it’s the right combination of form and function. I love the color, though there are three others available — Black, Artichoke, and Pewter — if the more traditional saddle color is a bit too bright.

My weakness is a great leather case for any phone, but unlike iPhone and Galaxy cases there aren’t many good Pixel options. There’s this $40 option made by Snakehive that I plan to pick up, but it lacks coverage on the top, bottom, and right button side, which I dislike. Still, it appears to have more supple leather than Bellroy’s, which should patina more quickly, so I’m looking forward to putting them head-to-head in the future.

Until then, I’m quite happy with Bellroy’s leather Pixel 11 Pro XL case, and plan to keep it on my phone until something else newer, shinier, and patina-ier comes along.

title: The Googlebook has an opportunity to build Android like nothing else [Video]
snippet: Despite having effectively zero market share right now, there is an opportunity for Googlebook to do something that basically nobody else could do, but can they do it? more…
fullText:
Despite having effectively zero market share right now, there is an opportunity for Googlebook to do something that basically nobody else could do, but can they do it?

I’ll state right up top that I’m already cautiously optimistic. We need a competitor player to Mac and, in particular, Windows. Microsoft, as of late, has been nothing but combative with the people who use the firm’s operating system every single day. A new player is needed. I’m still not fully convinced yet by Googlebooks, but there is an opportunity, a big opportunity that hinges on quite a few things falling into place.

Considering how many new products are released every year, it’s quite surprising how few operating systems are unveiled. I suppose there is a caveat that Android has existed for a long time, but there have been no true attempts to make it work as a “proper desktop” experience, save Samsung’s DeX system, which was an internal attempt to make it work with Galaxy phones and tablets.

For more video content, subscribe to 9to5Google on YouTube.

	

DeX is a fine take on things, but it is limited by virtue of being an experience trying to emulate a desktop experience. Googlebook OS is Android reimagined for the desktop era.

I’m still not sure if this is too late or if there is enough interest. Google’s move comes at a very interesting time. Maybe its impending launch was the reason that Chrome OS has languished in recent years, having had lots of early promise and a surging user base, particularly in the education sector.

I have had the benefit of trying out Googlebooks, but in the lead-up to launch, I’ve been thinking more broadly about why now, and whether there is any real, tangible reason that Google would fully adopt Android across phones, tablets, and, now, desktops/laptops.

Bear with me, though, as a lot of assumptions have to be made for my points to fully hit home. I know that isn’t ideal, but just indulge me in this thought exercise at the very least.

The high-end might not be the ‘tip of the spear’

We’ve just seen a slew of expensive hardware unveiled under the Googlebook branding. These are the “optimum” hardware experiences, and I do think many are overpriced. That’s not where I see the benefits.

Compared to previous Chrome OS versions, Android devices are better optimized for low-power, low-resource use. A bad Chromebook is almost always worse than a bad Android device, at least in my experience. It’s harder to hide bad performance on a laptop or desktop because you’re used to certain power thresholds. On a tablet or phone, that isn’t as pronounced because things are almost always more lightweight.

It helps that many Android SoCs are powerful enough now to rival mid-range desktop processors or at least those found in notebooks.

Android seems to scale much better now than a few years ago, but as Apple has shown recently, you can run desktop-level applications on mobile SoCs. I could easily see a laptop running absolutely fine with a Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 from a few years ago and doing so with very low power consumption.

Just a few years ago, when Google Stadia was still around, the idea of a “gaming Chromebook” felt silly and wasteful. Those machines relied entirely on the cloud, meaning you were paying a premium for a laptop that couldn’t actually play games without perfect Wi-Fi. However, if we get gaming Googlebooks these could be a very different prospect. 

Hardware has evolved to the point where modern mobile processors easily outperform last-generation consoles like the PlayStation 4, bringing entry-level gaming power straight into a laptop chassis without needing an internet connection.

At the same time, the software side has improved drastically. Android gaming is no longer just for casual mobile apps; it now features massive, high-fidelity games that look and feel like console titles. Combined with the ability to emulate older PC and console games locally, a gaming Googlebook becomes a genuine, self-sufficient gaming machine you can actually take anywhere, and one that doesn’t require a wall outlet to play for hours at a time.

Unlike Steam Machines and the Steam Deck, Fortnite is there right from day one.

Something else to consider that I think has been glossed over by basically anyone, because we’re so accustomed to mouse and keyboard interactions with a laptop or desktop.

No other desktop-level operating systems have been developed from the ground up with touch interactions in mind. This is one of the other major USPs for Googlebooks; I’ve already said it multiple times in this rundown that Android only needs to close an application gap. That is exponentially easier than trying to shoehorn a legacy OS into a new form factor.

Apple has kept iOS, iPadOS, and MacOS all as separate OS builds. Google’s “everything is Android” approach could be a masterstroke. I’m resting heavy emphasis on “could” in that equation.

Why? Well, there is a generation of people out there who have grown up effectively “mobile first.” Kids who are now young adults, the “iPad kids” that are now getting to a stage where they are looking for a product that is familiar, comfortable, and does everything they need.

They’ve grown up already using tools like Capcut rather than Adobe. Playing mobile games or mobile ports of the biggest games, like Roblox. Traditional desktop paradigms have never catered to those young people. Googlebooks and the Android experience, rightly or wrongly, extend the familiar to a new form factor. It’s a play that I haven’t seen many discuss, but that could work if the price is right.

‘Desktop-level’ could bring even wider benefits

For the older folks, we have a bee in our bonnets about “desktop-level software”. It’s still essential that we get some things ported over sooner rather than later.

If, for instance, Blackmagic or Adobe port over their respective software packages, Davicini Resolve or Creative Cloud apps to Googlebook, that’s great. 

There’s a hidden secondary benefit, though. The next wave of foldable phones with potential support for desktop apps or desktop app scaling now have access to professional-grade applications in a form factor that is multiple times more portable than a traditional laptop. This extends to tablets, too.

I’m quite bullish that Android tablets could be one of the biggest beneficiaries with the introduction of the Googlebook, that is, if the company is willing to allow more power tools to come to the other versions of Android that the Googlebook OS is based on.

You can rebuke much of what I have said for any number of reasons, but everyone can agree that so much hinges on which brands are willing to start building for Android. Closing this “app gap” is arguably the most important component of the Googlebook during its first year.

I’m cautiously optimistic about the Googlebook program. A fully flexible, malleable operating system that spans regular smartphones, foldables, tablets, laptops, and potentially desktops could do something no other OS has offered before. Scalable in ways that not even Apple has been able to do, but has half-stepped toward since making iPadOS a midway experience or bridge between iOS and Mac.

If Google invests in and enhances Android across the entire stack, every existing and future device will evolve at a rate that wasn’t possible before. Scalable for any screen size. Apps that can be desktop-level while still being mobile native.

There is a big “if” here, and that is the only reason I’m not fully invested yet. The current, glaring software gaps need to be plugged – and plugged fast.

There is a parallel that might prove to be a good omen. Linux has had a massive swell of users over the past year, driven by Valve and, in particular, Steam OS. The success of the Steam Deck has proven that an alternative to Windows can work for gamers.

I’m not sure if we’ll ever get a compatibility layer in Android for various Windows or Linux applications, but who knows. It is not out of the realm of possibility, and if it happens, it’s going to be a major turning point. Google just has to be sure that this is a long-term project, and improving on Chrome OS is a must.

Proton has done wonders for Valve over the past 3 or 4 years. This is a blueprint Google could follow. I do think getting native ports for a few of the biggest applications is all it will take to get more on board. A small swell could quite easily become a bigger wave of app conversion.

A few years ago, if you’d asked me if my gaming PC would ever run an OS other than Windows, I’d have said “never”. I sit here 18 months after ditching it in favor of Linux’s performance gains.

That experience has taught me to be less dismissive of Android on desktop than I was some months ago, and my time playing with the first run of Googlebooks has me excited for what might be coming next for Android.
